Methods in Molecular Biology

Methods in Molecular Biology

Damien Nevoltris Patrick Chames

Preface

The use of antibody-based therapeutics has grown exponentially in the past few decades, now representing a large component of therapeutic drugs that was dominated by small organic molecules up until the late 1990s. Antibodies have proven versatile in treating a varietyofdiseasesincludingcancer, autoimmunity, infectious diseases, orevenneurodegenerative disorders. As of 2017, 70 therapeutic antibodies have been approved by the FDA, and more than 550 promising candidates are in different phases of clinical trials. They currently represent 20% of the top 100 selling drugs, up from just 1% in 2007. However, major improvements and breakthroughs have been necessary to achieve these impressive results. The1970swerethestartofgreatrevolutionsinthefield:GeraldEdelmanandRodney Porter were awarded the Nobel Prize for their work on the molecular structure of antibodies, the first atomic resolution structure of an antibody fragment was published, followed by the groundbreaking development of hybridoma technology by Georges J. F. Ko¨hler and Ce´sar Milstein. This technology allowed antibodies to be produced and characterizedasmonoclonals, startingthemodern eraofantibodyengineering. Despite this revolution, the success of antibodies as therapeutic molecules was not immediate, and most clinical studies led to disappointments. First murine antibodies used as treatment had many limitations, such as a short in vivo half-life, limited tumor penetration, inefficient recruitment of host effector functions, and most of all, immune response from the patient against the injected antibody, also called “HAMA” response, referring to theproductionofneutralizinghumananti-mouseantibodies. For manyyears, researchersdevelopedstrategiestoabrogatethisproblem;thejourney towardantibodyhumanizationbegan. Fullymurineantibodiesfirstprogressedtochimeras, wherevariableregions frommurineoriginwereassembledontohumanconstantdomains, thentohumanizedantibodiesbyinsertionofonlytherelevantCDRsontohumanantibody scaffolds. Finally, fully human antibodies were generated, directly in genetically modified mice, selected from human synthetic antibody libraries or by sequencing of human plasma cells. However, immunogenicity was not the only factor holding up the development of antibodies. Indeed, the classical architecture of immunoglobulin molecules bears some inherent limitations. Many innovative formats have been explored to overcome these major hurdles, such as reducing the antibody to its minimal functional size, modulating thevalency, the(multi)specificity, increasingthehalf-life, andenhancingtherecruitmentof immuneeffectorcells. Asthedemandformonoclonalantibodiesinresearchandclinicalapplicationscontinues to increase, the necessity to develop even more efficient molecules is crucial. Antibody engineering has become a key discipline for generation of innovative antibodies-based moleculesusedinresearch, diagnostics, andtherapy. ThisthirdeditionofAntibodyEngineering:MethodsandProtocolsremainsinthelineage of its predecessors and gives the readers complete and easy access to a variety of antibody engineering techniques. From the generation of native, synthetic, or immune antibody libraries, the selection of lead candidates thanks to different powerful and innovating display technologies, totheirproduction, characterization, andoptimization, thishandbook providesthereaderwithanextensivetoolboxtocreatethepowerfulmoleculesoftomorrow. Darlinghurst, NSW, Australia DamienNevoltris Marseille, France PatrickChames

Keywords Antibody design, Humanization, De-immunization, Antibodyhomologymodel, PIGS, Rosetta, Antibodymodel, PredictionofImmunoglobulinStructures, Mouseantibodyhumanization, Homologymodel-guidedhumanization, Structure-basedantibodyengineering 1 Introduction Historically, antibodies have been generated mainly using mouse models. These antibodies worked best for research and diagnostic applications, butdidnotfarewellinhumantherapeuticuse. Inthe early days of therapeutic antibody development and use, mouse monoclonal antibody against a specific cancer target was administered directly to human patients. This led to generation of human anti-mouse antibody response (HAMA), which not only neutralized this therapeutic antibody but also led to severe allergic

4 VinodhB.KurellaandReddy Gali reactioninhumans. ResearchersthenreplacedmouseFc(fragment crystalline)andpartofFab(fragmentantigenbinding)withhuman antibody sequences, a chimeric antibody. This chimera, based on the sequence, did reduce overall immunogenicity of the mouse mAbbutstilldidcontainsubstantialmouseresidues.Greg Winter atMedicalResearchCouncil(MRC, UK)cameupwithanovelidea of taking the mouse CDRs of both heavy and light chains and transplanting them directly onto a fully human antibody scaffold. In this method, CDRs arethe only sequences that are mouse, and the rest of the antibody contains human sequence. This technique ispopularlyknownasCDRreplacement[1].Itwasagroundbreakingtechniqueatthattimeandisstillconsideredagoldstandardin antibody humanization. Over theyears, therehavebeennumerousmethodsdeveloped forundertakingantibodyhumanizationorantibodyde-immunization. Although CDR replacement dramatically reduces the mouse residues in the humanized antibody, however, in most cases it results in a significant drop in affinity toward the antigen. This is due to sequence and structural differences between mouse CDRs being supported by non-native human frameworks. Therefore, humanization becomes an iterative process in which numerous designs have to be made, tested, and ranked based on functional readout (e.g., affinity measurement). Itinvolvesreplacementofonlythoseresidues to human germline sequences, which are not conserved between mouse and human. Another technique involves a more conservative approach, inwhichreplacementisdoneonlyforoneframework at a time instead of all the four frameworks [2]. In this approach, designsaretested, andsequentialframeworkreplacementofmouse to human is accomplished, driven by affinity measurements and functional data. Framework shuffling is a method to create humanized antibody variants based on sequence conservation and randomization of heavy and light chains from different variable chain germline sequences [3]. Super humanization is another technique in which mouse CDRs are also humanized along with the frameworks [4]. Given HAMA responses against a mouse mAb are antibody mediated, researchers have mapped out the surface-exposed residues in the mouse mAb and replaced only those with corresponding human sequences, also known as antibody resurfacing [5]. This is achieved by delineating surface-exposed residues using either X-ray/NMR structures or homology model of the mousemAbfragmentvariableregion(Fv).Recently, thisapproach is further optimized, in which the mouse mAb Fv model is first generated, andthennon-conservedresiduesinmousearemutated to reflect human germline sequences. Thisapproach iswelladoptedbythescientificcommunityasahomologymodelguidedantibodyhumanization[6–9]. 1.1 Antibody Antibodies can be classified into canonical and noncanonical clas- Structures ses. Antibody heavy chain can be further divided into four frameworks, which encompass CDRs (H1, H2, H3) and light chain containing CDRs (L1, L2, L3). All these frameworks have a very highdegreeofsimilarstructuralfold.CDRsL1–L3andH1andH2 can be assigned to canonical classes. Based on the length and sequence, these loops can be modeled based on the structural templates available from these canonical classes in protein data bank. Given the diversity and uniqueness of CDR H3, it does not belong to any canonical family. In the recent past, there has been plethora of antibody structures determined via NMR, X-ray crystallography, as well as cryo-EM techniques. Most of these antibodieshavesequenceandstructuralsimilaritybetweenthemthathas led to creation and development of different algorithms for antibodyhomologymodelprediction, asopposedtoresource-intensive experimentalstructuredetermination. Thesealgorithmsprimarilyuseantibodysequenceinformation to extract structural templates from protein data bank (PDB), which results in creation of homology model of an antibody. Given tremendous growth in biologics in the recent past over small molecules, different researchers, as well as commercial companies, have developed antibody model prediction algorithms. PublicallyavailableantibodymodelingalgorithmsareRosettaantibody modeling, Web antibody modeling (WAM), structure-based antibodypredictionserver(SAbPred),PredictionofImmunoGlobulin Structures (PIGS), and Kotai (antibody builder). Commercially, there are a number of antibody modeling products, such as Biovia’sDiscoveryStudio, Schrodinger’sBioLuminate, andChemical Computing Group’s MOE and Macromoltek. A brief descriptionofsomeofthesepredictionalgorithmsisdescribed. 1.2 WebAntibody Antibody modeling algorithm follows a series of steps to obtain a Modeling(WAM) homology model from the sequences of variable heavy and light chains. It consists of sequence-based search for framework and canonical loop regions to find the most homologous structure from protein data bank. Noncanonical antibody regions are built either using knowledge-based search from databases or ab initio model building, using CONGEN conformational search [10]. Final conformational homology model is selected from the fivelowestenergymodels, rankedbasedontorsionanglesclosestto theoriginalPDBtemplate.

As framework regions are mostly conserved across different antibodies, a framework3Dmodelisbuilt.CDR-H3structureisthemostvariableand challenging to predict; hence its structural fold is created by de novo model building. Once VH–VL orientation is chosen via sequence blast of the whole Fv (fragment variable—VH þ VL) against the PDB, the modeled CDR loops for VH and VL are grafted onto this framework template for further refinement and model building. Engrafted model is energy minimized, and an ensemble of high-resolution models <3000 are ranked based on Rosetta score that reflects probable entropies in each model, andthelowestenergyisrankedasthetopmodel[11]. 1.4 Prediction Ingeneral, thisantibodyvariablehomologymodelingserveralgoofImmunoglobulin rithm is similar to those mentioned above. However, there are Structures(PIGS) some differences in the workflow and strategies implemented in PIGS. A sequence-based analysis is performed to obtain homologous framework sequences of known antibody structures from protein data bank. Antibody CDRs with canonical loops are modeled based on known antibody structures and grafted upon the framework model. Bothheavyandlightchainmodels(iftheparental templates are different) then are packed together based on conserved interface residues at the heavy and light chains from known antibody structures. Finally, energy minimization of the side chains is carried out via SCWRL4.0 (side chain with backbone-dependentrotamer library),results in the finalantibody homologymodelgeneration[12]. 2 Materials Antibody humanization can be undertaken either using commerciallyavailabletools(Schrodinger’sBioLuminate, Biovia’sDiscovery Studio, Chemical ComputingGroup’s MOE and Macromoltek)or publically available web servers (Prediction of Immunoglobulin Structures-PIGS;Rosettaantibodymodeling;structure-basedantibody prediction server- SAbPred; and Kotai -antibody builder). To describe and delineate differences and limitations between these algorithmswillbebeyondthescopeofthischapter. Given, publically available resources and servers can be accessed by everyone with a computer and internet access. This chapter will primarily focus on utilizing public servers for antibody homology model building and humanization.

Antibody Affinity Maturation by Computational Design Daisuke Kuroda and Kouhei Tsumoto Abstract The immune systems protect our bodies from foreign molecules or antigens, where antibodies play important roles. Antibodies evolve over time upon antigen encounter by somatically mutating their genome sequences. Theendresultisaseriesofantibodiesthatdisplayhigheraffinitiesandspecificitiesto specific antigens. Thisprocessiscalledaffinitymaturation.Recentimprovementsincomputerhardwareand modelingalgorithmsnowenabletherationaldesignofproteinstructuresandfunctions, andseveralworks oncomputer-aidedantibodydesignhavebeenpublished. Inthischapter, webrieflydescribecomputational methodsforantibodyaffinitymaturation, focusingonmethodsforsamplingantibodyconformationsand forscoringdesignedantibodyvariants. Wealsodiscusslessonslearnedfromthesuccessfulcomputer-aided designofantibodies. Key words Antibody engineering, Affinity maturation, Computer-aided design, Molecular simulations, Sampling, Scoring 1 Introduction Computational methods are widely accepted as essential tools for drug discovery of small molecules, helping with tasks such as screening candidate compounds, evaluating drug-likeness, and optimizing physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties [1]. In these contexts, computational methods are generally not considered substitutes for “wet lab” experiments but rather are a way to generate testable hypotheses, thus helping to guide experiments and interpret the results. In recent years, computational methods have garnered much attention in regard to antibody research and drug discovery [2, 3]. The applications of those tools in this field include affinity improvement [4–7], specificity control [8], engineering for thermostability [9, 10], aggregation propensity[11,12],andhumanization[13–19].Inthischapter, we briefly review successes regarding improvingthe affinity of antibody–antigen interactions and discuss how potential affinity enhancing mutations might be identified. Antibodies play important roles in the immune systems. They 1.1 Antibody Structure recognize variety of foreign molecules or antigens, which in turn induce further immune responses to protect our body from external perturbation. The number of antigens is far more than the number of antibody genes, but several mechanisms, such as V(D) Jrecombinationandsomaticmaturation, existtoexpandthediversityofantibodies. Antibodieshaveamodulararchitecture, inwhich variable heavy (V ) and variable light (V ) domains form dimeric H L F domains (Fig. 1). Antigen-binding sites comprise six V complementarity-determining regions (CDR-L1, CDR-L2, CDR-L3, CDR-H1, CDR-H2, and CDR-H3) in the F regions, V wherein CDR-H3 is the most diverse and important for antigen recognition [22–25]. The number of antibody crystal structures has been rapidly increasing and now exceeds 2000 in the Protein DataBank(PDB)[26,27].Comparisonofthesecrystalstructures revealed that the conformations of CDRs other than H3 are relatively rigid and classified well into so-called canonical structures [20, 28–31]. The modular architecture of antibodies has been exploitedtohumanizeantibodiesbygraftingfunctionalnonhuman CDRsontohumanframeworkregions(FRs)[13] withsomeback mutations [32] and more recently to create several alternative bispecificantibodyformats[33].

To obtain epitope-specific antibodies, combiningdisplaytechnologieswithcomputationalstructuralmodelingis analternativeroute[53,54]. 2 Computer-Aided Protein Design Antibodies can be optimized by computational design with or without antigens. In the absence of antigen structures, computationaldesignenablesstabilityengineeringofantibodiesbyoptimizing the amino acid sequences of given starting structures of antibodies. With an antigen structure, computational design can consider an antibody–antigen interaction and optimize the interface, toincreasetheaffinityoftheantibodytowarditsantigen. Both stability- and affinity-enhancing mutations are crucial in antibody engineeringandthedevelopmentofbiotherapeutics. Computational protein design algorithms have improved steadily and have revealed several principles in protein architecture [55, 56]. Computational protein design relies on estimating changes in free energy due to amino acid substitution, which can be accomplished by using scoring functions, such as physics-based force fields or knowledge-based potentials derived from the structural database [57]. Protein design also requires efficient conformationalsearchalgorithms, oftenwithside-chainrotamerlibraries [58],tosampleconformationsofmodifiedstructures. Protein design can be classified into two categories: redesign and de novo design [59]. During redesign, scoring functions and conformational search algorithms can utilize information from a nativeproteinoraninterfaceasastartingpoint. Mostoftheinitial efforts of rational protein engineering involved redesign of the surface or interior of monomeric proteins, so that the existing monomers acquire better thermostability [60–62]. Later, computational design extended its ability to create a novel protein fold that does not exist in nature [63] and to alter protein–protein interfaces, thus achieving affinity maturation of protein complexes [64–67]. Several community-wide efforts have led to improvements in various computational modeling techniques [68–74]. Started in 2003, one such effort in the protein–protein docking field is the Critical Assessment of Prediction of Interactions (CAPRI) experiment [69]. In recent years, CAPRI has included evaluation of scoring functions to assess protein interactions toward better computational design algorithms [75, 76]. Founded on such efforts, severaldenovodesignsofproteininterfaceshaveemerged [77–83].Notably, BakerandcoworkersdevelopedaRosetta-based protocol, which grafts precomputed hotspots onto a protein

AntibodyAffinityMaturationbyComputationalDesign 19 scaffold, followed by optimization of surrounding amino acids [77, 83]. However, the resulting interfaces tend to have poor affinities(K >~μM)andoftenrequiresubsequentinvitroaffinity D maturation[83]tocompensateforburied, unsatisfiedpolaratoms atthedenovodesignedinterface. Boththesuccessesandfailuresof computationally designed protein interfaces have yielded insights regarding current design techniques [84]. For example, designed interfaces are smaller and more hydrophobic than those of native protein–proteincomplexes, highlightingthedifficultyindesigning buried polar interfaces. This drawback would be problematic in antibody designs, given that antibody–antigen interfaces tend to be more polar than other types of protein–protein interfaces [39]. Furthermore, the successful designed interfaces consist predominantly of regular secondary structures, such as α-helix and β-strand, whereas the antigen-binding sites of antibodies consist ofsixCDRloops, furtherspotlightingachallengeregardingcomputer-aidedantibodydesign. 3 Method Overview Table 1 lists the computational protein modeling tools that are freely available for academic research. Among them, the Rosetta designsuite[85]canaccomplishnumerousproteinmodelingtasks, from predicting protein structure to docking and design [63, 90–93]. Highly customizable scripting interfaces and web-basedRosettaapplicationsarealsoavailable[94–97]. 3.1 Choosing Computationalproteindesignstartswithchoosingcandidateposi- MutationalSites tions for mutation (Fig. 3a). For example, if the design goal is to stabilize a protein structure, one might focus on the protein core, such that side-chain arrangements within the protein can become more densely packed. Targeting surface residues is an alternative approach, especiallywhendesigningaggregation-resistantproteins. In this context, exposed hydrophobic residues are often deleterious, so mutations to charged residues might achieve aggregation resistant antibodies [98]. In terms of interface design, antigen-contacting residues are the primary candidates. As discussed in following sections, previoussuccessfulexamplesofinsilicoaffinity maturation of antibodies have targeted all residues in CDRs or in CDR-H3 [4–7, 99]. However, some residues in both FRs and CDRs are important for maintaining the canonical conformations of antibodies, and these key residues must be retained during design calculations. From our experience, unless intentionally excluded, these structure-determining residues are often mutated during computational design. Therefore, efficient antibody design must involve incorporating sequence–structure correlations into design algorithms.

After sampling, the resulting variants are ranked by using a scoring function, thereby focusing laboratory efforts: usually the top ten variants are chosen for further experimental study7.ThecomputationaltoolsinTable1canconcurrently sample and score protein conformations, thereby promptly generating designed variants. However, in principle, sampling and scoring can be uncoupled [103]. There are many side-chain samplingalgorithmsthatcouldbeusedinmutantside-chainprediction [104–107]. Rescoring modified structures by using a different scoring function sometimes yields better ranking of designed variants [75, 108]. MM-PBSA/GBSA is widely used for such rescoringpurposes[6]becauseofitsfavorablebalancebetweenaccuracy and computational speed. We provide the following several examples to illustrate how well current computational approaches have achievedthedesignofhigh-affinityantibodies. 4 In Silico Affinity Maturation of Antibodies Forthepastseveralyears, withafewnotableexceptions[109–111], mostoftheexamplesofcomputer-aidedantibodydesignareredesign of the amino acid sequences of antibodies toward better antigen binding [2]. Although some mutations in noncontacting regionsdoimprovebindingaffinity[40,112],computationalaffinitymaturation usuallyfocusesonantigen-contactingresidues (i.e., CDRs). Consequently the availability of crystal structures of antibody–antigencomplexesisanimportantfactorinachievingaffinity maturationofantibodiesinsilico. Notethatinthefollowingexamples, we have used the Chothia numbering scheme, which sometimes differs from the residue numbering in the original publications. 4.1 CaseStudy1 Guided by a complex’s crystal structure (PDB ID: 1MHP), Clark etal.optimizedanantibodyforbindingtotheIdomainofhuman integrin VLA1 [4] by using various computational methods, including the CHARMM22 force field [113] and ICE software [114]forscoringandCHARMM[115]andtheDezymersoftware thatusesaDead-EndElimination(DEE)-basedside-chainrepacking algorithm [116] for side-chain rotamer sampling. The authors testednearlyeveryantigen-contactingresidueinthecomputational designs. This approach achieved a tenfold improvement in the binding affinity over wild type (K: 850 pM versus 7 nM) D [4]. The authors primarily used competitive ELISA to measure binding affinity and assessed 83 designed variants, including some

22 DaisukeKurodaandKouheiTsumoto multiple-mutation candidates; a variant containing a combination offourmutations(L,S28Q,N53E;H,T50V,K64E)displayedthe highest affinity. Theauthorsalsodeterminedthecrystalstructureof the optimal variant and confirmed the intended rearrangement of thehydrogenbondnetworkintheinterface. 4.2 CaseStudy2 In another successful antibody–antigen redesign, Lippow et al. exploitedseveralcrystalstructuresofantibody–antigencomplexes, includingthoseofananti-lysozymeantibody, D44.1(1MLC),and an anti-EGFR antibody, cetuximab (1YY9) [5]. Similar to Clark et al. [4], they designed single mutations in all CDR positions by usingtheCHARMM22forcefield[113]forscoringandtheDEE and A* search algorithms for side-chain sampling. Experimental binding affinities were measured by using a yeast display method. The final ranking of the designed mutations involved using Poisson–Boltzmann electrostatics; this process resulted in a fourmutation combination (L, N92A; H, T28D, S56V, T57D) for D44.1 that provided a 100-fold improvement in affinity over wild type(43pMversus4.4nM),aswellasathree-mutationcombination(L:S26D,T31E,N93A)forcetuximabthatachievedatenfold improvement(52pMversus490pM). 4.3 CaseStudy3 To improve the affinity of trastuzumab for human epidermal growthfactorreceptor2(HER2),Lietal.introducedsinglemutations in all CDR positions by using a crystal structure of the complex (1N8Z) as a starting structure, a Monte Carlo-simulated annealing algorithm and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with the CHARMM22 force field [113] for sampling, and MM-PBSA calculations for scoring [6]. Among 11 designs, 2 variants(L,N30RandH, N54K)displayed~twofoldimprovedbinding affinity (as quantified by ELISA) compared with wild type (~92 pM and ~80 pM, respectively, versus 160 pM). The authors further improved the affinities (approximately ~threefold) and the designsuccessrate(from18.2%[2/11]to60%[6/10])bytargeting peripheral positions at the interface and by restricting the candidate amino acids manipulated during the design process to thosefrequentlyobservedthroughsomaticmaturationinvivo. The most affinity-enhancing mutation was D98Y at the heavy chain. Testinganotherantibody–antigencomplexaswellasnon-antibody interfaces, the authors generalized their design strategy and drew thefollowingtwoconclusions:(1)mutationpositionsshouldbeat theperipheryoftheinterface, and(2)substitutingresiduesshould be those that are frequently used during antibody affinity maturationinvivo. Inaddition, theauthorsfoundthataffinity-enhancing mutations tend to cluster around particular nucleotide positions, “hotspots,”wheresomaticmutationsoftenoccurinvivo.

AntibodyAffinityMaturationbyComputationalDesign 23 4.4 CaseStudy4 Bindingaffinityisnotthesoleparameter forrationalimprovement of functional antibodies. For antiviral antibodies, neutralizing potency and breadth are key parameters in rational design. In this regard, WillisandcoworkersappliedtheRosettasoftwaresuite[85] to a crystal structure of the complex between the neutralizing antibody PG9 and the V1/V2 domain of HIV-1 gp120 (3U4E) tomanipulateallpositionsofCDR-H3[99].Theirdesignledtoan antibodythatshowedenhancedneutralizingpotencyandbreadth, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) showed that its enhancedneutralizingcapacityresultedfromtheincreasedthermostabilityduetothedesignedmutation, N100 Y,atCDR-H3. F 4.5 CaseStudy5 In line with advances in computational design algorithms, we started with the structure of an antibody–antigen complex (11K2 and MCP1, respectively) in the PDB (2BDN) to improve the affinity of the interaction by using a computational saturation mutagenesis approach [7]. We used the program MODELLER of the Discovery Studio suite (Accelrys, San Diego, CA) to sample antibody structures, and the final scoring of variants was based on interaction energies, which we assessed through the AMBER99 force field as implemented in MOE (Chemical Computing Group, Canada). As seen for previous interface designs [4, 6, 67, 117],thisapproachidentifiedseveralaffinity-enhancingmutations thatwerelocatedattheperipheryoftheinterface(L,N31R,S53E, S53D, T56E, T56D); interestingly, all of these mutations were mutations to charged residues. The most effective mutation (L: N31R) showed 4.6-fold improved affinity over wild type (170pMversus800pM). 4.6 Lessonsfrom The examples provided above are proof-of-concept studies that Successful imply that—when crystal structures are available—current scoring functions and associated sampling algorithms can be sufficiently Computational Designs accurate for improving antibody–antigen interfaces through computationalsaturationmutagenesis. AsshowninFig.4,current computer-aided antibody designs demonstrate improvements in affinityfromapproximatelynanomolartopicomolarlevels. Because | the backbones | | in the | cited examples | | were | not | altered beyond | | | ————- | — | —— | ————– | — | —- | — | ————– | — | energy minimization, these successes also highlight the validity of fixed-backbone assumption during computational design in the presenceofantigens. However, noncontactingresiduescanchange due to mutation in the corresponding germline genes during in vivomaturation (Fig.2),whereasprevious insilico affinity maturation efforts have focused on antigen-contacting residues only. Computationaldesignstargetingnoncontactresiduesneedtoconsiderallostericeffects, inwhichbackbonemovementiscritical. A clear lesson learned from the aforementioned studies is that targetingperipheralresiduesispromisingforaffinitymaturation. In particular, incorporating charged residues at the periphery of the

24 DaisukeKurodaandKouheiTsumoto

Fig. 4 Experimental ΔG values (binned in 0.5-kcal/mol increments) of 191 antibody–antigen complexes compiled from the PDB through the SAbDab [26]. These complexes were divided based on antigen types (protein, peptide, others). Empty circles, approximate ΔG values of wild types; shaded circles, approximate ΔGvaluesofrepresentativedesignedvariants interface isdesirable, given that explicitly incorporating the effects ofwatermoleculesduringthedesignprocessremainsdifficult, and desolvation effects would be smaller at the periphery than at the center of interfaces. These observations are consistent with the O-ring hypothesis of protein–protein interfaces, in which interaction hotspots are clustered in the centers of interfaces and surrounding residues protect hotspots from contact with the bulk solvent [118, 119]; as a result, the centers of binding sites are wellburiedandtightlypacked. Therefore, theseburiedhydrophobic residues may already be well optimized for specific antigen binding, suchthatthesurroundingresiduesoffergreateropportunitiesforincreasingaffinityandfurtherimprovingantigenbinding. 5 Structure-Based Benchmark for Antibody Affinity Maturation Theaforementionedsuccessfulexamplesexploiteddifferentdesign strategies for different antibodies. A standard benchmark set is desirable, to assess and generalize design strategies [108, 120, 121]. Because of the importance of antibody–antigen interactions inbiomedicalresearchandindustry, numerousmutagenesisstudies of such complexes have been carried out [122]. Oberlin et al. compiled such existing experimental mutagenesis data and benchmarked DEE/A* for side-chain sampling and MM-PBSA with Boltzmann averaging of multiple conformations for scoring [123]. Applied to the 173 mutations of 7 complexes (anti-VAL1

AntibodyAffinityMaturationbyComputationalDesign 25 antibody, D44.1, D1.3, HyHEL-63, cetuximab, bH1, and Barnase–Barstarcomplex),theirprotocolyieldedasuccessrate(percentageofcorrectpredictionsregardingthesignonΔΔGinthesets)of 45%. One comprehensive benchmark set for assessing protein–protein interactions is SKEMPI, which comprises 3047 binding free energy changes due to mutation [120]; in particular, SKEMPI includes more than 300 mutations of antibodies whose structures areavailableinthePDB.Anothercomprehensivebenchmarksetis the AB-Bind database compiled by Keating and coworkers [121], which includes 1101 mutations of antibody and antibody-like molecules for which experimental binding energies and the structural information are available. Keating and coworkers used the AB-Bind to benchmark several scoring functions (DFIRE [124], dipolar DFIRE [125], STATIUM [126], FoldX [86], Discovery Studio [Accelrys, San Diego, CA], and Score12 in Rosetta [63]), showing that thecorrelationsbetween predictedand experimental ΔΔGvaluesareratherlow(r¼0.16–0.45). Large-scaledatasetmakesmachinelearningmethodsattractive for antibody design, such that affinity-enhancing mutations could be identified from sequence and structural information based on features learned from existing benchmark sets. Although most current scoring functions for protein design have been derived from experimental information of general protein structures, an antibody-specific scoring function has been also developed. In brief, Pires and Ascher proposed an antibody-specific graph-based method, mCSM-AB, which evaluated the geometry and physicochemicalpropertiesofantibody–antigencomplexesbyconsidering atoms as nodes and interactions as edges [127]. For the AB-Bind set, mCSM-AB yielded better correlations between predicted and experimentalΔΔGvalues(r~0.56)thanonesreportedbyKeating andcoworkers[121]. 6 Perspectives Computer-aidedantibodydesignisbecomingincreasinglyfeasible. Although most antibody design projects to date have focused on redesigning existing antibodies and antibody–antigen complexes, recent improvements in computer hardware and modeling algorithms now enable de novo design of the structures and functions of proteins [55, 63, 77–83, 93], including antibodies [109–111].Recently, Fleishmanandcoworkersdevelopedanantibodydesignalgorithm, AbDesign[128].Thisalgorithmassembles various backbone segments of natural antibodies and, during design, exploits sequence constraints derived from a position specific scoring matrix (PSSM) of multiple sequence alignments of natural antibodies. This knowledge-based constraint helps to

26 DaisukeKurodaandKouheiTsumoto mimic natural antibody sequences, thereby retaining structure-determining residues in antibody structures during sequence design. However, antibodiesdesigneddenovobyusingAbDesign had some structural defects and low expression levels; manual optimization with FoldIt [129] and error-prone PCR procedures were necessary to improve antigen binding [111]. Creating hotspotsdenovo, asantibodiesdoinvivo, isevenmorechallenging. Inaddition, protocolsforbothsamplingandscoringantibody structuresneedfurtherimprovements. Backbonesamplingremains a major challenge in computational design, especially when the design goal is to simultaneously improve binding affinity and stability. Althoughmostofthesuccessfulredesignsforaffinitymaturations have held the backbones of the antibody and antigen nearly rigid, we have experienced difficulties during stability engineering of antibodies with fixed backbone assumption: in the absence of antigen structures, computationalsaturationmutagenesisofentire F domains often suggests mutations in both FRs and CDRs. V However, our experience has shown that thermostability often improves when mutations are introduced in FRs but not in CDRs. This is most likely due to the assumption of a fixed backbone during computational design: without antigen structures, CDRs are more flexible than FRs. Therefore, even though the suggested mutations in CDRs might stabilize a given fixed backbone, flexible CDRs might move due to mutations, leading to destabilized, deformed antibodies. This observation suggests that fixed-backbone approximation is invalid especially in the absence of antigens. In addition, we have found that even when the stabilityenhancingmutationsarefarfromthebindingsites, thebindingcapabilities of antibodies often decrease. In contrast, when an antigen structure is present, CDRs directly interact with the antigen and acquire some rigidity, thus making the fixed-backbone assumption validtoacertainextentininterfacedesign. Tosimultaneouslyimprove bindingaffinityandstability, incorporatingbackbonemovementinto computer-aidedantibodydesignalgorithmswouldbeakeyadvance. Community-wide efforts highlight directions in development of scoring functions [75, 76]. Ideally, thebest variant predictedin silico corresponds to the antibody with the best binding affinity in vitro or in vivo, so that human labor is minimal (i.e., where testing only a single variant confirms that it is an ideal antibody). One attractive method for compensating for defects in scoring functions is structure-based library design, in which, based on structures of an antibody–antigen complex, computational design techniquesrestrictthesequencespaceofantibodiesforsubsequent invitromaturationandletnatureselectidealaminoacidsfromthe limited set of residues to increase antigen binding [53]. In the absenceofcrystalstructuresofantibodiesandantigens, homology modeling and the subsequent protein–protein docking could be exploited to build a design input [130]. Antibody modeling

AntibodyAffinityMaturationbyComputationalDesign 27 protocolsareimprovingsteadily[72],andsub-angstromaccuracies havebeenachieved, evenwhenmodelingCDR-H3[131]. Albeit computationally expensive, the most rigorous physicsbasedapproachforassessingbindingfreeenergiesisMD-basedfree energy perturbation (FEP) methods. Recently, Friesner and coworkersappliedaFEPmethodtocomplexescomprisingneutralizing antibodies and the gp120 envelope glycoprotein of HIV-1 to predict the binding free energy changes upon alanine mutation [132]. The authors’ FEP method significantly outperformed FoldX (correlation between predicted and experimental ΔΔG [r2]: 0.62 versus 0.15). Although the cited work is only a case studyofafewrelatedantibodiesandasingleantigen, givenrecent advances in computational power, sampling algorithms, and force fields [133–135], high-throughput MD-based binding energy assessmentsofantibody–antigencomplexesmaysoonbecomeroutine.MDsimulationsarealsousefulforinterpretingcomputational designandexperimentalresults. RecentdevelopmentsofMDuser interfaces, such as CHARMM-GUI [136], make it easier for non-experts to perform MD simulations. Unlike conventional design simulations, MD simulations can produce time-dependent trajectoriesofproteinstructuresandsuggestalternativehypotheses thatcanbetestedthroughfurtherlaboratoryexperiments. Finally, a recent study proposed a sequence-based statistical inference method to predict binding affinity of antibodies based on a maximum entropy model [137]. Under an assumption that matured antibody sequences with high existing probability are morelikelytohavehigherbindingaffinityfor theantigen, amaximum entropy model was trained on deep sequencing data of a HIV-1-infected patient [138]. For the 20 HIV-1 isolates, the correlation (r) between the predicted scores and IC neutraliza-50 tion titer measured on 30 antibodies was as high as 0.77. The success of Asti et al. shed light on the value of next-generation sequencing(NGS) datain antibodyengineering.NGS analyses on the adaptive immune systems are opening a new avenue for the studyofimmunerepertoires[139],andinterpretationofthehuge amountofNGSdatawillbefurtherenhancedbystatisticalmodels [140]. Together with recent advances in antibody modeling [37], those NGS data will advance our understanding in the immune systemsinunprecedenteddepthandenabledenovoengineeringof antibodystructuresandfunctions. ® Use of IMGT Databases and Tools for Antibody Engineering and Humanization Marie-Paule Lefranc, Franc¸ois Ehrenmann, Sofia Kossida, Ve´ronique Giudicelli, and Patrice Duroux Abstract ® ® IMGT,theinternationalImMunoGeneTicsinformationsystem (http://www.imgt.org),wascreatedin 1989byMarie-PauleLefranc(Universite´ deMontpellierandCNRS)tomanagethehugediversityofthe antigen receptors, immunoglobulins (IG) or antibodies, and T cell receptors (TR). The founding of ® IMGT marked the advent of immunoinformatics, which emerged at the interface between immunoge- ® netics and bioinformatics. Standardized sequence and structure analysis of antibody using IMGT databases and tools allow one to bridge, for the first time, the gap between antibody sequences and threedimensional(3D)structures. ThisisachievedthroughtheIMGTScientificchartrules, basedontheIMGT- ONTOLOGYconcepts ofclassification (IMGTgeneandallelenomenclature), description (IMGTstan- ® dardized labels), and numerotation (IMGTunique numbering and IMGT Collier de Perles). IMGT is acknowledgedastheglobalreferenceforimmunogeneticsandimmunoinformatics, anditsstandardsare ® particularlyusefulforantibodyengineeringandhumanization.IMGT databasesforantibodynucleotide sequences and genes include IMGT/LIGM-DB and IMGT/GENE-DB, respectively, and nucleotide sequence analysis is performed by the IMGT/V-QUEST and IMGT/JunctionAnalysis tools and for ® NGSbyIMGT/HighV-QUEST.Inthischapter, wefocusonIMGT databasesandtoolsforaminoacid sequences, two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) structures: the IMGT/DomainGapAlign andIMGTCollierdePerlestoolsandtheIMGT/2Dstructure-DBandIMGT/3Dstructure-DBdatabase. IMGT/mAb-DB provides the query interface for monoclonal antibodies (mAb), fusion proteins for immuneapplications(FPIA),andcompositeproteinsforclinicalapplications(CPCA)andrelatedproteins of interest (RPI) and links to the proposed and recommended lists of the World Health Organization InternationalNonproprietaryName(WHOINN)programme, toIMGT/2Dstructure-DBforaminoacid sequences, and to IMGT/3Dstructure-DB and its associated tools (IMGT/StructuralQuery, IMGT/ DomainSuperimpose)forcrystallizedantibodies. Key words Antibody humanization, IMGT-ONTOLOGY, IMGT, IMGT Collier de Perles, Paratope, Bcellepitope, Vdomain, Cdomain, Immunoglobulin, IMGTuniquenumbering 1 Introduction ® ® IMGT, the international ImMunoGeneTics information system (http://www.imgt.org) [1], was created in 1989, by Marie-Paule

36 Marie-PauleLefrancetal. Lefranc, in Montpellier, France (Universite´ de Montpellier and CNRS), in order to standardize the immunogenetics data and to managethehugediversityoftheantigenreceptors, immunoglobulins (IG)orantibodies, andTcellreceptors(TR)[2,3].Thefoundingof IMGT ® markedtheadventofimmunoinformatics, whichemergedat the interface between immunogenetics and bioinformatics [4]. IMGT ® is acknowledged as the global reference in immunogenetics and immunoinformatics [5–13] and its standards have been approved by the International Union of Immunological Societies ® (IUIS)NomenclatureCommittee[14,15].IMGT providesacommonaccesstostandardizedandintegrateddatafromgenome, prote- ® ome, genetics, and three-dimensional (3D) structures. IMGT comprisessevendatabases(forsequences, genes, and3Dstructures), 17 online tools, and more than 20,000 pages of Web resources [1] ® (Fig. 1). The accuracy and the consistency of the IMGT data are basedonIMGT-ONTOLOGY, thefirstontologyforimmunogenet- ® icsandimmunoinformatics[16–26].IMGT providestheinformatics frameandknowledgeenvironmentforastandardizedanalysisofthe antibody sequences and 3D structures, in the context of antibody engineering (single-chain fragment variable (scFv), phage displays, combinatorial libraries), antibody specificity, affinity and effector properties, and antibody humanization (chimeric, humanized, and humanantibodies)[27–38]. The analysis of IG or antibody and TR nucleotide sequences ® representsakeycontributionofIMGT andisperformedwiththe IMGT/V-QUEST tool [39, 40] and the integrated IMGT/JunctionAnalysis software [41]. Customized parameters and results provided byIMGT/V-QUESTand IMGT/JunctionAnalysis have beendescribedelsewhere[42–45].SinceOctober2010,theanalysis of IG or antibody and TR nucleotide sequences obtained from next-generation sequencing (NGS) (or high-throughput sequencing(HTS),deepsequencing)canbeperformedbyIMGT/HighV- | QUEST | [46–50] | that analyzes | | up to 500,000 | | sequences | per run | | —– | ——- | ————- | — | ————- | — | ——— | ——- | (including scFv [51, 52]), identifies and compares IMGT clonotypes (AA) between batches (up to one million sequences), and provides outputs for further diversity and expression statistical analysis by IMGT/StatClonotype [53, 54]. These tools compare usernucleotidesequencesagainstIMGTreferencedirectories, built ® from data from IMGT/LIGM-DB, the IMGT nucleotide sequence database [55], and from IMGT/GENE-DB, the ® ® IMGT gene database [56]. In this chapter, we focus on IMGT databases and tools for amino acid sequences, two-dimensional (2D) and 3D structures [57–65]: the IMGT/DomainGapAlign and IMGT Collier de Perles tools and the IMGT/2Dstructure- DB and IMGT/3Dstructure-DB database. IMGT/mAb-DB [1, 66] provides the query interface for therapeutic monoclonal antibodies(mAb),fusionproteinsforimmuneapplications(FPIA), composite proteins for clinical applications (CPCA), and related

These databases and tools were built, as all other IMGT components, usingtheIMGTScientificchartrulesgeneratedfrom theIMGT-ONTOLOGYaxiomsandconcepts.

38 Marie-PauleLefrancetal. 2 IMGT-ONTOLOGY 2.1 IMGT-ONTOLOGY The Formal IMGT-ONTOLOGY [23] comprises seven axioms, AxiomsandConcepts “IDENTIFICATION,” “CLASSIFICATION,” “DESCRIP- TION,” “NUMEROTATION,” “LOCALIZATION,” “ORIEN- TATION,”and“OBTENTION”,whichpostulatethatanyobject, any process, and any relation has to be identified, classified, described, numbered, localized, and orientated and that the way itisobtainedcanbecharacterized. Conceptsgeneratedfromthese axioms [16–26, 67–74] have allowed the implementation of the IMGT Scientific chart rules http://www.imgt.org/ ® IMGTScientificChart/, used in the IMGT databases and tools. Thus the axioms “CLASSIFICATION,” “DESCRIPTION,” and “NUMEROTATION” have generated the concepts of classification (IMGT gene and allele nomenclature), description (IMGT standardizedlabels),andnumerotation(IMGTuniquenumbering ® andIMGTCollierdePerles)whicharewidelyusedintheIMGT aminoacid,2Dand3Ddatabases, andtools[57–65]. 2.2 IMGT-ONTOLOGY The IMGT-ONTOLOGY concepts of classification, with the ® Conceptsof IMGT geneandallelenomenclature, gavebirthtoimmunoinfor- Classification:IMGT® matics, anewscienceattheinterfacebetweenimmunogeneticsand GeneandAllele bioinformatics [4]. Indeed, for the first time, immunoglobulin Nomenclature (IG) or antibody and T cell receptor (TR) variable (V), diversity (D), joining (J), and constant (C) genes were officially recognized as“genes”aswellastheconventionalgenes[4].Thismajorbreakthrough allowed IG and TR genes and alleles of the complex and highly diversified adaptive immune responses to be managed in ® genomic databases and tools. The IMGT gene nomenclature [2, 3, 75, 76] was approved at the international level by the Human Genome Organisation (HUGO) Nomenclature Committee(HGNC)in1999[77,78]andendorsedbytheIUISNomenclatureCommittee14,15.TheIMGT ® IGandTR gene names are the official reference for the genome projects and, as such, have been entered in IMGT/GENE-DB [56], in the Genome Database (GDB) [79], in LocusLink at the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) [80], in Entrez Gene (NCBI) when this database (now designated as “Gene”) supersededLocusLink[81],intheNCBIMapViewer, inEnsembl at the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI) [82], and in the Vertebrate Genome Annotation (Vega) browser [83] at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute (UK). Amino acid sequences of the human IG and TR constant genes (e.g., Homo sapiens IGHM, IGHG1, IGHG2) were provided to UniProt in 2008 and those of the human IG variable genes with their IMGT gene definition (e.g.,HomosapiensIGHV1–2immunoglobulinheavyvariable1–2) in 2016 [84]. Their ® Description:IMGT definitionsareavailableontheIMGT Website(http://www.imgt. ® Standardized Labels org). Labels are used in IMGT databases and tools and allow a detailedanalysisofthenucleotideandaminoacid(AA)sequences, 2D and 3D structures. Sequences have to be gapped according to the IMGTunique numbering (using, e.g., IMGT/DomainGapAlign) (see Subheading 3). IMGT/Collier-de-Perles tool can be customized to display the CDR-IMGTaccording to their IMGT Color menuor theFR-IMGTaminoacidsaccordingtotheirhydropathy or volumeclassesor tothe11IMGTphysicochemicalclasses[96] (IMGTAide-Me´moire, Aminoacids, http://www.imgt.org). 5 IMGT/2Dstructure-DB In a further effort to bridge the gap between sequences and 3D structures, anextensionofIMGT/3Dstructure-DB, designatedas IMGT/2Dstructure-DB, was created to describe and analyze amino acid sequences of antibodies for which no 3D structures are available [32]. These amino acid sequences are analyzed and ® managed with the IMGT criteria of standardized nomenclature, description, and numerotation. IMGT/2Dstructure-DB uses the IMGT/3Dstructure-DB informatics frame and interface (see Subheading6)whichallowtoanalyze, manage, andqueryantibodiesas polymeric receptors made of several chains, in contrast to the IMGT/LIGM-DB sequence database that analyzes and manages IG sequences, individually. The current IMGT/2Dstructure-DB entries include amino acid sequences of antibodies from Kabat (those for which thereare noavailable nucleotide sequences) [91] and aminoacidsequencesof-mab and -ceptfromtheWHO INN programme31,85.Queriescanbemadeon anindividualentry, usingtheEntryID(e.g.,foranINNentry, the four-number code, e.g., 8693) or the Molecule name (e.g., for an INN entry, the INN, e.g., motavizumab). Search can be made on Entry type (e.g., “INN”) (Fig. 6) and by using selected IMGT- ONTOLOGY concepts (detailed in the Query page, http://www. imgt.org). The IMGT/2Dstructure-DB cards provide standardizedIMGTinformationonchainsanddomainsandIMGTColliers de Perles on one or two layers as described below (see Subheading 6); however, the information on experimental structural data (hydrogen bonds in IMGT Collier de Perles on two layers, contact analysis) is only available in the corresponding IMGT/3Dstructure-DB cards, if the antibodies have been crystallized.

In IMGT/ 3Dstructure-DB, the “IMGT paratope and epitope” section for IG/Ag complexes is determined by combining contact analysis with an interaction scoring function. They are described in a standardizedway. Thus, theAgepitopeof3ixt(Fig.9)comprisesAAof Fusion glycoprotein F1 (3ixt_P). Eleven AA form the Ag epitope. EachAAthatbelongstotheepitopeisdefinedbyitspositioninthe chaininthe3Dstructure(iftheAAispartofaV, C,orGdomain, the position is given according to the IMGT unique numbering [88–90]). IMGT®forAntibodyEngineeringandHumanization 61 International Congress of Immunology in San Francisco (CA, USA),IMGT-NC(createdin1989andworkingwiththeIUIS Nomenclature Committee since 1992) became officially the IUIS Nomenclature Subcommittee for immunoglobulins (IG) and T cell receptors (TR) (IMGT-NC) [14, 15]. IMGT geneandallelenamesarebasedontheconceptsofclassification of “Group,” “Subgroup,” “Gene,” and “Allele,” generated from the IMGT-ONTOLOGY CLASSIFICATION axiom [68]. 2. The variable (V) domain includes the V-DOMAIN of the IG and TR and the V-LIKE-DOMAIN of the immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF) proteins other than IG and TR [87, 88]. The constant (C) domain includes the C-DOMAIN of the IG and TR and the C-LIKE-DOMAIN of the IgSF proteins other than IG and TR [89]. The groove (G) domain includes the G-DOMAIN of the major histocompatibility (MH) and the G-LIKE-DOMAIN of the MH superfamily (MhSF) proteins other than MH (or related proteins of the immunesystem(RPI)-MH1Like)[90]. 3. Theframeworkcomprisestheantiparallelbetastrands, ninefor 0 00 theVdomains(A,B,C,C,C,D,E,F,G)andsevenfortheC domains(A,B,C,D,E,F,G). 4. “3ixt” is the code of a 3D structure entry in the Research Collaboratory for Structural Bioinformatics (RCSB) Protein Data Bank (PDB) [102] or “PDB code” (comprising four ® letters and/or numbers). IMGT uses the “PDB code” as “IMGT entry ID” for the 3D structures in IMGT/3Dstructure-DB, http://www.imgt.org [61–63]. An additional letter separatedbya“_”identifiesthedifferentchainsina3Dstructure. For example, the 3ixt entry, the 3Dstructure of anIG / antigen (Ag) complex (motavizumab Fab in complex with the antigen “ligand” Fusion glycoprotein F1), comprises the following chains: 3ixt_A and 3ixt_H (VH-CH1) and 3ixt_B, 3ixt_L (L-KAPPA) for the IG Fab, and 3ixt_C and 3ixt_P for theantigen(“ligand”). 5. Anchor positions, first defined for V domains, belong to the strands (or FR-IMGT in V-DOMAIN) and represent 0 00 “anchors” supporting the three BC, CC, and FG loops (CDR1-IMGT, CDR2-IMGT, and CDR3-IMGT, respectively, in V-DOMAIN). Anchor positions for V domains (V-DOMAIN of IG and TR and V-LIKE-DOMAIN of IgSF otherthanIGandTR)arepositions26and39,55and66,and 104 and 118 [87, 88]. By analogy, six anchor positions were defined in C domains [89]: positions 26 and 39, 45 and 77 (delimiting the characteristic transverse CD strand of C domain), and 104 and 118 [89] (which structurally corresponds to J-PHE or J-TRP of the IG and TR J-REGION [2, 3]). Anchor positions are shown in squares in the IMGT CollierdePerles. 7. IMGT color menu for the CDR-IMGT of a V-DOMAIN indicates the type of rearrangement, V-J or V-D-J [2, 3]. Thus, the IMGT color menu for CDR1-IMGT, CDR2- IMGT, and CDR3-IMGT is red, orange, and purple for VH (encoded by a V-D-J-REGION resulting from a V-D-J rearrangement) and blue, green and green blue for V-KAPPA or V-LAMBDA(encodedbyaV-J-REGIONresultingfromaV-J rearrangement). The assignment is done automatically by IMGT/DomainGapAlign[62,64]. 8. In IMGT-ONTOLOGY, the CDR-IMGT length is used instead of the canonical structure. Indeed, (1) most identified (15 out of 19) canonical structures correspond to a given

IMGT®forAntibodyEngineeringandHumanization 63 CDR-IMGT length; (2) only 2 CDR-IMGT lengths have 2 canonical structures (CDR1-IMGT of 9 AA of IGLV and CDR2-IMGTof8AAofIGHV);(3)canonicalstructureshave not been identified for every CDR-IMGT length (“n.d.” in Fig. 13); (4) many “variants” are described in the literature, based only on sequences and without experimental evidence; (5)canonical structurescannotbeidentified forCDR3owing totheirdiversityinlengthsandsequencesandtotheirflexibility; and (6) canonical structure identification is reliable only if 3Dstructuresareknown.Thus, theCDR-IMGTlengthisthe mostaccuratewaytodefinethethreeCDR, whileworkingon sequences, that information being completed with characteristicsResidue@Position(Subheading6.2),ifnecessary. Construction of Human Na¨ıve Antibody Gene Libraries Michela Pasello, Alessandra Mallano, Michela Flego, Silvia Zamboni, Anna Maria Giudice, and Katia Scotlandi Abstract Size and variability often represent an obstacle in generating an effective antibody gene library for the detectionofanabundantrepertoireofantigens. Therefore, optimizingtheconstructionofalargelibraryis essentialfortheselectionofhigh-affinityreactivefragments. Here, wereportahighlyefficientmethodfor the construction of a human na¨ıve antibody gene library for the selection of antibodies as single-chain variable fragments. Thisprotocolisbasedonmanydifferentsetsofoligonucleotideprimersandmultistep electroporationandligationreactions. Thisadvancedmethodcanbeadoptedbyanymolecularbiologylaboratorytogenerateana¨ıvelibraryfor useinisolatingsingle-chainfragmentvariablesagainstspecifictargets. Keywords Antibody, Single-chainvariablefragment, scFv, Phagedisplay, Naivelibrary, Biopanning, Nonimmunelibrary 1 Introduction An antibodygene library is a valuable resourcefor the selection of antibodies for many basic research, diagnostic, and therapeutic applications. The key to obtaining good antibodies is the antibody gene libraryusedforselectioninbiopanningexperiments[1]. In the past, different gene libraries, including naive, immune, synthetic, and semisynthetic libraries, have been generated [2–6]. In particular, to isolate human antibodies against viruses, microbeparticles, andtumor-associatedantigens, immunelibraries might be constructed from immunized/infected patients. These immune libraries represent relevant immune reagents for medical research, since they increase the probability of selecting antibodies thatcouldbeusedfortherapy[7,8].Unfortunately, themolecular andgeneticaspectsofimmunelibrariesrepresentabiologicallimitation since the construction of a new library is required for each antigen. Furthermore, theavailabilityofhumanimmunelibrariesis

74 MichelaPaselloetal. limited due to ethical reasons, although this approach might be partiallyextendedtononhumanprimatesconsideringthesimilarity or theirantibodygenestohumanantibodygenes[9]. In contrast, different types of antibody gene libraries (nonimmune or naive libraries) can be designed and developed from natural sources using RNA extracted from the peripheral lymphocytes[10],bonemarrow[11],andspleentissues[12].Intheory, it ispossibletoselectantibodieswithdifferentspecificitiesusingonly oneofthese“universal”libraries. However, thescreeningofhuman repertoires of in vivo rearranged V genes from nonimmunized individuals for antibodies that bind to specific antigens has occasionally generated results inferior to those obtained with the same antigen by screening an immunized donor library. Generally, the affinities of fragments isolated from small naive libraries are lower thanthoseisolatedfromlargerlibraries[13]. Thus, thesize ofthe libraryisimportantfor theselectionofhigh-affinityfragmentsand to determine the success rate of selecting phages against a large repertoireofdifferentantigens[14]. Formanyapplications, themostversatileantibodyformatisthe single-chain variable fragment (scFv) in which the variable regions ofheavy(VH)andlightchains(VL)ofimmunoglobulins(Vgenes) arejoinedtogetherbyalinker. ThescFvsareconsideredthebuilding blocks for the construction of more complex and effective antibodies. Here, we proposed a method to construct human naive scFv antibody libraries with high affinity and variability. Because the protocolsemployedtoconstructlibrariescouldaffecttheirquality, size, and functionality of these resources, the method proposed herein combines various improvements to generate a high-quality biotechnological tool. Each critical step (V gene amplification, primersetdesign, ligation, andelectroporationreactions)wasoptimizedtopreservesamplevariability. 2 Materials 2.1 PeripheralBlood l Phosphate buffered saline (PBS) pH 7.4: 8 g NaCl, 0.2 g KCl, MononuclearCell 1.44gNa HPO *2H O,0.24gKH PO in1L. 2 4 2 2 4 (PBMC)Isolation, Total l Histopaque-1077(Sigma-Aldrich). Onesub-libraryiscomposed ofthreedifferentdonorsamples. Thecombinationofsub-libraries composes the complete library, and new sub-libraries can easily be added with a consequent increase in both the number and variabilityofantibodiesthatcanbeselectedinbiopanningexperiments therebyincreasingandimprovingthesizeandqualityofthelibrary. The protocol for the construction of a human scFv library is optimizedtomaximizetheyieldofeachcriticalstep(Vgeneamplificationfromasingledonor, optimizedprimerset, reducedstepsof ligation, andelectroporation). The first step involves the amplification of immunoglobulin V genes from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from (λ/κ) human healthy donors and the assembly of VH–VL fragments by two-step PCR using specific primers. The primers for V genes were designed and constructed according to Sblattero and Bradbury[15]andmodifiedasreportedinPaselloetal.[6].

LibraryConstructionProtocol 79 Foreachsample76differentPCRreactionswillbeperformed. Subsequently, equimolarmixturesforeachchain(VH, Vλ,andVκ) will be generated, each containing a pool of three donors. The mixtures of VH and VL (λ/κ) chains, obtained from the same three donors, will be combined and assembled by a second PCR reaction step to obtain the scFv antibody. This step included a PCR-like reaction to assemble the chain fragments and a subsequent standard PCR reaction to amplify the scFv. In the PCR-likereaction, equimolaramountsofallheavyandlightchains will be joined between the overlapping ends of the linker, posi-0 0 tionedatthe3 endofVHandthe5 endofVL.DNApolymerase adds the lacking nucleotides in the 5 0 –3 0 direction VH–V(λ/κ). s s Subsequently, thedifferentscFvmoleculesobtainedinlaststepwill beamplifiedbyasecondclassicPCRreactionwithprimersanneal-0 0 ing at the 5 end of VH and 3 end of VL ends. The obtained fragments will be used in the following ligation with the pDNS expression vector [6]. All DNA ligation products obtained from each single pool (three donors) will be used for different simultaneous bacterial transformations. The clones from one pool represent one sub-library. Each sub-library will be used to produce phages. The ensemble of phages from each pool represents the completephagelibrary. TheprotocolworkflowisshowninFig.1. 3.1 PeripheralBlood 1. Construction of Synthetic Antibody Libraries De´borah Caucheteur, Gautier Robin, Vincent Parez, and Pierre Martineau Abstract Librariesofantibodyfragmentsdisplayedonfilamentousphagesarenowawidelyusedapproachtoisolate antibodies against virtually any target. We describe a simple protocol to make large and diverse libraries basedonasingleoralimitednumberofframeworks. Theapproachisflexibleenoughtobeusedwithany antibodyformat, eithersingle-chain(scFv, VHH)ormulti-chain(Fv, Fab,(Fab0)2),andtotargetinasingle step the six complementarity-determining regions—or any other part—of the antibody molecule. Using thisprotocol, librarieslargerthan1010canbeconstructedinasingleweek. Keywords Kunkelmutagenesis, Antibodyfragment, Single-chainFv, Phagedisplay, Syntheticlibrary 1 Introduction Withmorethan50moleculesalreadyregistered, humanmonoclonalantibodies(mAbs)haveprovedtheir valueastherapeuticmolecules in numerous pathologies [1–3]. These mAbs are usually obtainedthroughthreemaintechnologies[4,5]:miceimmunization followed by hybridoma generation and then in vitro humanization; transgenic mice genetically engineered for producing human antibodies [6];and in vitro methods such as phage, ribosome, or yeast display [7]. The display-based methods present several advantages over the animal-based ones, in particular their lowcost, highflexibility, andhighspeed, andfortherapeuticapplications, their ability to directly generate human antibodies and human-mousecross-reactingmAbsforthepreclinicalcharacterizationsinrodentmodels. Among the display methods, phage display is currently the mostwidelyusedapproachandhasprovedtobeacheapandrobust technology. Thisisparticularlythecasewhenanaivelibraryisused, sinceasingleantibodysourceisusedforalltheprojects. Forsimple selections, antibodies against any target can be identified in about 2weeks, andthemethodcanbeautomatedandruninparallelwith several antigens [8]. However, few naive and diverse phage-

94 De´borahCaucheteuretal. displayedlibrariesarepubliclyavailable, andthefirststepisthusto develop your own antibody source. For this critical step, you can rely on the natural diversity of human-recombined antibodies by cloning them from a collection of healthy human donors, or you can design the library using structural and sequence information and build it in vitro using molecular biology techniques [9–12]. The former has the advantage of using natural genes but requiresmanystepsandhumandonors, whereasthelatteronlyuses in vitro techniques but requires a careful design to obtain efficient libraries. Most of the phage-displayed libraries use antibody fragments like scFv, Fab, or VHH fused to the g3p filamentous phage capsid protein. Inaddition, mostauthorsuseaphagemidsinceitiseasier to manipulate than phages and essentially results in a monovalent display of the antibody fragment, allowing a more stringent selection than the multivalent display obtained when using phage vectors. SincethepioneeringworkofDr.Kabat[13],itiswellknown that most of thediversity of the antibodymolecule isfound inthe six complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), three being located in each chain. Because of their critical role in the antibody-antigen interaction, these six regions are the main target for randomization in most synthetic library designs. However, the averagecontributionofthesixCDRstothebindingenergyisvery variable, the heavy chain CDR2 and CDR3 being the main contributors, andthelightchainCDR2onlyrarelyinteractingwiththe antigen. In addition, there is also a strong bias in the amino acid distribution in the natural antibody paratopes with a high abundance of tyrosine residues. Using these information may lead to cleverer library designs, but this requires a flexible mutagenesis methodtoconstructthem[11]. Inthisprotocol, wewilldescribetheconstructionofasynthetic library, based on a unique framework. We will add diversity in the 6CDRloopsandlengthvariationsintheVHCDR3.Theprotocol is based on the well-known site-directed mutagenesis method developed by Dr. Kunkel [14]. The main interest of this approach is that the library is constructed in a single step using a pool of randomizedoligonucleotidesandcanaddressanyantibodyformat. WewillintroducediversityinthesixCDRs, buttheprotocolcanbe easilyadaptedtoalsointroducediversitytoframeworkregions, toa more restricted number of positions, or using a restrained amino acidcode. 2 Materials All buffers must be prepared with ultrapure water and ACS grade chemicals and stored at room temperature unless otherwise indicated.

Construction of Histidine-Enriched Shark IgNAR Variable Domain Antibody Libraries for the Isolation of pH-Sensitive vNAR Fragments Doreen Ko¨nning, Steffen Hinz, Julius Grzeschik, Christian Schro¨ter, Simon Krah, Stefan Zielonka, and Harald Kolmar Abstract The adaptive immune system of sharks comprises a heavy chain-only antibody isotype, referred to as immunoglobulinnewantigenreceptor(IgNAR).AntigenbindingincaseofIgNARantibodiesismediated byasinglevariabledomain(vNAR).Duetotheirinherentbeneficialbiophysicalproperties, suchassmall sizeandhighthermalstabilitycombinedwithahighspecificityandaffinitytotheirtargetantigens, vNAR domainsemergedaspromisingtoolsforbiotechnologicalandbiomedicalapplications. Herein, wepresent detailedprotocolsfortheengineeringofpH-sensitivityintoIgNARVdomainsbyconstructinghistidineenriched and CDR3-diversified semisynthetic antibody libraries which can then be screened upon using yeastsurfacedisplay. ProtonationordeprotonationofincorporatedhistidineresiduesatdifferentpHvalues resultsinstructuraltransitionscausedbyalteredelectrostaticinteractions. Theseinteractionsaccountforan alteredbindingbehaviortowardthetargetantigen. Inthefollowingprotocol, wedescribethegenerationof a semisynthetic vNAR master library that comprises two histidine residues on average in the 12-residue CDR3loop.Moreover, onceapH-dependentvNARpopulationtowardthetargetantigenisidentified, this population can further be optimized in terms of affinity and pH sensitivity upon conducting a CDR1mediatedaffinitymaturation. Keywords Shark, IgNAR, vNAR, Yeastsurfacedisplay, Antibodyengineering, Proteinengineering, Librarygeneration, pH-dependentbinding, Singledomainantibody 1 Introduction Besides classical hetero-tetrameric antibodies composed of heavy andlightchains, sharksproduceaheavychain-onlyisotype, termed IgNAR, which does not associate with light chains [1, 2]. The antigen-bindingsiteofeachchainofIgNARiscomposedofasingle domain, referredtoasvNAR(IgNARV),whichisfollowedbyfive constant domains. Like conventional antibody domains, the IgNAR V domain consists of a classical immunoglobulin fold [3].However, vNARentitiesdisplayseveraluniquefeatures, clearly

110 DoreenKo¨nningetal. distinguishing them from camelid VHH domains. Due to a deletion in the framework2-CDR2-region, IgNAR V domains only

have two | complementarity | | determining | | regions, | CDR1 | and |

CDR3(Fig.1)[4].Yet, attheCDR2truncationsite, theremaining surface exposed loop wraps around the molecule in a “belt-like” structure. It was shown that after antigen contact, somatic hypermutation also occurs in this region namely in a loop which corresponds to HV4 in T-cell receptors, to which vNAR domains share structuralsimilarity. Consequently, theseregionshavebeentermed HV2 and HV4, respectively [5]. Peculiarly, vNAR domains also exist as T-cellreceptor fusion proteins, supporting the notion that | IgNAR | plays a role | in both | the | immunology | | of T cells | and B | | —– | ———— | ——- | — | ———- | — | ———- | —– | cells[6]. Variable domains of IgNAR can be divided into four different types, categorizedbasedonthenumberandpatternofnoncanonical disulfide bonds that are typically not found in conventional Fig.13DdepictionofavNARantibodyfragmentshowingatransparentsurface combinedwitharibbonrepresentation. TheCDR1(red)andCDR3(blue)binding sitesarehighlighted. ThenoncanonicaldisulfidebondbetweenCDR1andCDR3 andthecanonicaldisulfidebondconnectingtheframeworkregionsareshownin yellow. GenerationofHistidine-EnrichedSharkvNARLibraries 111 antibody domains [7–11]. This results in an unprecedented repertoire of different loop structures that represent the paratope of IgNAR V domains [12]. In addition, the convex architecture of the paratope of vNAR domains seems to be predisposed to target also clefts of the antigen. Such recessed epitopes are usually notantigenictoconventionalantibodies[11,13–15].Furtherbeneficial attributes of the vNAR domain comprise its high thermal stability as well as tolerance to irreversible denaturation [16–18]. Accordingly, target-specific vNAR molecules have been isolatedagainstawiderangeofdisease-relatedantigens[16–24].It wasdescribedrecentlybyourgroupthatIgNARVdomainscanbe engineeredtowardpH-sensitivebindingbehavior[25].Ingeneral, the engineering of pH sensitivity into proteins, antibodies, and antibody-derived fragments in particular has attracted substantial interest with respect to biomedical and biotechnological applications. Such pH-switchable molecules can, for instance, be utilized foraffinity chromatography wheretheproteinofinterest isbound atpH7.4andelutedfromthestationaryphaseuponreducingthe pH to 6.0 [26, 27]. With regard to biomedical applications, the antibodycouldbeengineeredtowardbindingoftumor-associated antigensspecificallyintheacidictumormicroenvironment. Suchan antibody should comprise high affinity for its antigen at slightly acidicpH, butverylowaffinityatneutralpH, therebyincreasingits specificity and, ultimately, the therapeutic window [28]. Furthermore, theengineeringofapH-switchintoanantibodymoietycan be utilized to modulate its half-life and, thereby, its pharmacokinetic profile. Toward this end, Igawa and coworkers engineered pH-dependent IL-6 receptor-targeting antibodies that only engaged their target at neutral but not acidic pH [29–31]. Upon binding to the IL-6 receptor, the receptor-antibody complex is internalized, and the pH-engineered antibody is able to release thereceptorintheacidicmilieuofthelysosome. Whilethereceptor is subjected to the degradative pathway, the antibody is recycled back into the circulation and can undergo another round of internalizationandrecycling[32]. In our own study, we reported the isolation of pH-sensitive IgNAR variable domains from a semisynthetic master library. To thisend, ahistidine-dopedmasterlibrarywasconstructedwithtwo histidine residues on average in a fully randomized 12-residue CDR3 binding site. Selection over several rounds for binding at pH 7.4 and for decreased binding at pH 6.0 yielded several single clones which showed specific and pH-dependent binding to their antigens. Inthischapter, weprovideaprotocolforlibraryestablishment of histidine-doped semisynthetic CDR3-randomized shark vNAR antibodydomainlibrariesforyeastsurfacedisplaythatarebasedon the natural IgNAR repertoire of the bamboo shark (Chiloscyllium plagiosum).

114 DoreenKo¨nningetal. 3 Methods

In the following section, we will thoroughly describe the steps which are required for the generation of a semisynthetic, CDR3randomized, and histidine-enriched vNAR library based on the natural repertoire found in the bamboo shark. This library will subsequently be sampled using yeast surface display as platform technology. In that manner, blood samples from nonimmunized bamboo shark specimen need to be harvested, followed by the isolation oftotal RNAfrom whole blood samples. Afterwards, the cDNAhastobepreparedandthelibraryhastobegeneratedusing a generic three-step PCR methodology (Fig. 2). Alternatively, the library can also be constructed from a single bamboo shark vNAR sequence as a template, rather than using the whole, na¨ıve Fig.2SchematicrepresentationofthePCR-basedlibrarydesign.PCR-amplifiedvNARfragmentsfromblood circulating lymphocytes of a bamboo shark or, alternatively, a DNA fragment encoding a defined vNAR sequence are used as template for CDR3 randomization. In a first PCR reaction, the vNAR framework is amplified. TheCysresidueinCDR1isreplacedbyTyr, andamarginaldiversityisintroducedusingtheforward primer. DuringthesecondPCR, theCDR3iscompletelyrandomized, andoverhangsforgaprepaircloningin yeastor, alternatively, restrictionsitesforcloningintoaphagemid(notshown)areattachedduringthethird andlastPCR

GenerationofHistidine-EnrichedSharkvNARLibraries 115 repertoire (see Note 1). However, we recommend starting with a pool of different vNAR scaffolds. It has been reported that minor sequencevariations foundin thescaffoldsequences, suchas inthe framework regions, may have a large impact on protein folding stability as well as solubility [34, 35]. Display Technologies for Generation of Ig Single Variable Domains Vladimir Bobkov, Bas van der Woning, and Hans de Haard Abstract Variablefragmentsofheavy-chain-onlyantibodies(VHH)foundincamelidsarevaluableresearchtoolsin pharmacologyandbiotechnologyandarebeingdevelopedfortheclinictotreatpatientswithautoimmune andinfectiousdiseasesorcancer. Theirsingle-domainnatureandbiochemicalpropertiesgreatlyfacilitate the development process. The most common technology to select single-domain antibody fragments is phagedisplayfollowingactiveimmunizationofllamasorothermembersofCamelidaefamily.Selectionof VHHfromimmunephagelibrariesisarapidapproachtodiscoverabroadpanelofinvivomaturedantigenspecific clones with comprehensive functionalities. In this chapter, we describe a detailed protocol for construction of VHH immune libraries and phage display selection against antigens in their native conformation. Key words Phage display, Single-domain antibody, Heavy-chain-only antibody, Camelidae, VHH, Nanobody, Immunelibrary, Virus-likeparticle 1 Introduction Since the discovery of heavy-chain-only antibodies (HCAbs) in llamas in 1993 by Hamers-Casterman et al. [1], the potential of single-domainantibodies, alsocalledvariableheavy-chainregionof a heavy-chain only antibody or VHH, has been widely explored in the treatment and diagnosis of cancer and infectious and autoimmune diseases, as well as in structural and functional studies of GPCRs [2–4]. Unlike the conventional antibodies, the HCAbs of camelids lack CH1 domain and cannot pair with light chains. Therefore, variable fragments of such HCAbs are represented by small, about 15 kDa, single-domain VHH, which can be easily expressedrecombinantlyinprokaryoticsystemswithfullyretained antigen-bindingpropertiesandexcellentstabilityinsolution. Their single-domain nature and favorable biochemical properties make them ideal candidates for an affinity selection via in vitro antibody display.

Toraiseaspecificimmuneresponseinllamas, animmunization step can be performed by various methods depending on a target and its available forms. The most straightforward approach is immunization with purified recombinant protein. Nevertheless, many transmembrane targets are dependent on the cellular membrane to maintain a correct native conformation and are generally not available as purified full-length proteins. In this case, immunization with cells or lipoparticles overexpressing the protein of interest can be used as an alternative method. Additionally, DNA immunization approach was successfully applied for generating an immuneresponseagainstthetargetswithmultipletransmembrane domains such as GPCRs [5, 6]. The advantage of immunization with recombinant protein or DNA over whole cell immunization consists in the lack of non-specific off-target immune response against multiple components of the injected cells, which are also exposedtotheimmunesystemofllamas. After immunization, RNA is isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC), and VHH fragments, undergone somatic maturation, can be rescued in a single PCR step. After cloning into a phage vector, single variable domain antibody fragments are fused to the minor coat protein pIII (see Fig. 1). Direct coating of a recombinant protein results in the immobilization of many more copies of target molecules as compared to the coating of cells or lipoparticles, where only a limited number of target molecules are present, making the avid phage binding a major advantage during theselectionstep.
