A Streamlined Approach for the Construction of Large Yeast Surface Display Fab Antibody Libraries Simon Krah, Julius Grzeschik, Simon Rosowski, Ramona Gaa, Iris Willenbuecher, Deniz Demir, Lars Toleikis, Harald Kolmar, Stefan Becker, and Stefan Zielonka Abstract Yeastsurfacedisplayisaversatileplatformtechnologyforantibodydiscovery.Nevertheless, theconstructionofantibodyFablibrariestypicallyisatediousmultistepprocessthatinvolvesthegenerationofheavy chainaswellaslightchaindisplayplasmidsindifferenthaploidyeaststrainsfollowedbyyeastmating. Here, wepresentafocusedone-stepGoldenGatecloningapproachforthegenerationofyeastsurfacedisplayFab librariesthatallowsforsimultaneousintroductionofheavy-chainandlight-chainvariableregionsintoone singledisplayvector. Thereby, theoveralltimeaswellasthematerialsneededforlibrarygenerationcanbe reducedsignificantly. Keywords Yeastsurfacedisplay, Antibodyengineering, Proteinengineering, Hitdiscovery, Golden Gatecloning, Fabfragment, Librarygeneration 1 Introduction Yeast surface display (YSD) is a versatile platform technology for antibody as well as protein engineering [1]. Developed by Boder and Wittrup in 1997, the genotype-phenotype coupling relies on the genetic fusion of the antibody-encoding DNA sequences in-framewiththeAga2p matingadhesion receptor ofSaccharomyces cerevisiae. Display of the antibody on the yeast surface is facilitatedthroughcovalentlinkageofAga2ptoAga1pthatisanchored tothecellwall. Tothisdate, yeastsurfacedisplayhasbeensuccessfully applied for many applications such as antibody affinity maturation, antibody stability- and pH-engineering, and selection of SimonKrahandJuliusGrzeschikcontributedequallytothiswork.

146 SimonKrahetal. antibody repertoires from na¨ıve and synthetic sources as well as fromimmunizedanimals[2–6].Additionally, alsononclassicalantibodies as well as non-antibody scaffolds were engineered by YSD [7–13]. Utilization of the eukaryotic host S. cerevisiae ensures a proper protein folding due to the presence of quality control machineries, enabling co-selection of high-level expression as well as stability simultaneously to the binding functionality. Moreover, its compatibility to fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) enablessinglecellreal-timeandonlineanalysisaswellascharacterizationofindividuallibrarycandidates[14]. Usingyeastsurfacedisplay, antibodyScFvdisplaycanbefacilitated by the expression of the binding moiety from one single plasmidandantibodylibrariesaretypicallygeneratedinahomologous recombination-based process named plasmid gap repair [15–18]. However, the classical approach for the display of Fab fragments, [19] which more resemble the structure of an IgG, is complex, relying on the individual generation of heavy and light chainplasmidsviaplasmidgaprepairinhaploidyeaststrains. Afterward, these haploid yeast cells are combined to diploid cells that display functional Fab fragments on their surface in a process referred to as yeast mating [2, 5]. Although this technology allows for the efficientgeneration of largeantibodylibraries, this - three-step process of library construction is tedious and timeconsuming[20]. In2008,anovelcloningtechnologywaspresented, referredto asGoldenGatecloning[21].Thiscloningstrategyhasitsoriginsin 1996, when it was shown that multiple DNA fragments can be clonedintoaplasmidbytheuseoftypeIIsrestrictionsenzymesand T4 DNA ligase [20, 22, 23]. Such restriction enzymes cleave outside of their recognition site, resulting in a DNA overhang which can be composed of any nucleotide sequence, and consequently those overhangs (herein termed as signature sequences) can be designed by purpose. Marillonnet and co-workers demonstratedthiscloningprinciplebydesigningthecleavagesitesandthe resulting overhangs of two DNA fragments in a way that both digestedfragmentswereligatedtoaproductinaseamlessmanner, i.e.,therestrictionsiteswereeliminatedinthefinalproductduring restrictionandligation[21].Thisallowedforsubcloninginasingle stepandasingletubewithaparamountcloningefficacy. Compared toconventionalrestrictionenzyme-basedcloning, afurtheradvantage is that signature sequences can be composed of different distinct sequences. By carefully designing complementary overhangs, several DNA fragments can be cloned in a directional fashion. Moreover, religation of respective vectors can be prevented [21].Consequently, itwasshownthatuptotendifferentfragments canbeassembledinadefinedorder for thegenerationofshuffling

SelectionofAnti-StructuredDNAAntibodyFragments 159 3. In general, signature sequences were part of constant compo- nents of the display system. SigA was part of the N-terminal region of CL kappa. Consequently, when light chain constant region lambda is desired, this sequence needs to be adjusted accordingly(alsoinoligonucleotide).SigBwas“buried”inthe sequence of signal peptide APP8, whereas SigC was “hidden” inthesequenceofAga2psignalpeptide.Finally, SigDwaspart oftheN-terminalregionofIgGdomainCH1.Whenworking with synthetic libraries, make sure that BsaI recognition sites are absent in your scaffoldsequence. Alternatively, otherType IIsrestrictionenzymescanbeutilized. 4. Typically, one electroporation reaction into EBY100 yields in approximately 2 107 to 5 107 unique clones. Scale-up golden gate reactions by parallelization to obtain a sufficient librarysize. 5. Sequencing primers can be designed from sequences given in Note1.Werecommenddesigningtheprimersinawaythatthe VH as well as the VL region will be covered by two independent sequencing runs. To this end, oligonucleotides should anneal 40–60 bp upstream of the corresponding variable region. 6. In general, labeling steps are performed with 107 cells in a volume of 20 μL. For library sorting purposes, scale-up in order to be able to sample a sufficient number of clones. By increasingthenumbersofcells, volumesandamountsoflabeling reagents should be increased proportionally. We recommend to oversample the generated diversity by the factor of 10. However, when large libraries are being generated, the limiting factor is throughput by FACS. For the first round of FACS, a maximum number of cells should be sorted. For subsequent sorting rounds, we typically oversample the numberofisolatedcellsfromthepreviousroundbythefactorof10. 7. Amultitudeoflabelingreagentsarecommerciallyavailableand different combinations of fluorescent dyes and detection reagents can be combined. With respect to fluorophore selection, it should be considered that excitation and emission spectra do not overlap. Otherwise, appropriate compensation needs to be applied on the FACS device. Guidance should be givenbytherespectivemanufacturer. 8. To enhance stringency, the antigen concentration can be reducedsignificantly. However, werecommendtostartsorting at an antigen concentration of 1 μM for initial rounds and to stepwisely reduce the concentration as soon as cells are enrichedforanantigen-bindingpopulation. 9. When working with nonimmunized antibody repertoires, dif- ferent secondary detection reagents should be alternated in order toavoidenrichmentofoff-targetbinders.

Keywords Phagedisplay, Antibodyfragments, Selection, Screening, Biotinylation, Soluble, Magnetic beads 1 Introduction Phage display is a robust in vitro selection method that is widely used to select binders from large libraries of up to 1010 different clones[1–5].Theprincipleofphagedisplayreliesonaphysicallink between a protein to be selected and its gene [6]. The gene of 0 interestisfusedto5 endofthep3geneoffilamentousphageM13, leadingtoparticlesexpressingattheirtipap3N-terminallyfusedto the protein of interest. Binders can be selected by incubating the whole library with the antigen of interest, washing out irrelevant phages and eluting binders. These selected clones can be used to infectE.coli, allowingaproductionofphageenrichedwithbinders andreadytobeusedinasubsequentselectionround. Onceseveral rounds of selection have been performed, individual clones can be picked to produce monoclonal preparation of phage particles in 96-well plates. These preparations can be used to perform an ELISA-based screening assay. A variation of this procedure can be performedusingculturesupernatantcontainingthesolubleprotein non-fusedtothephageparticle.

166 MagaliColazetandPatrickChames While it has been shown that selection can be performed on a variety of antigen source including purified antigens [7, 8], lysates [9], intact cells [10–12], or tissue sections [12, 13], selection on purified antigen remains the easiest and most effective approach. However the outcome of such selection can be greatly influenced bythewaytoimmobilizetheantigenofinterest[14,15].Indeed, one of the most straightforward approaches consists in the direct adsorptionofthepurifiedantigenonaplasticsurfacesuchasawell of a microtiter plate or an immunotube. This approach does not relyonanyproteinmodificationbutrequiressomeconformational changeoftheproteintobeadsorbedtoexposehydrophobicinterfaces toward the plastic [16]. As a consequence, some binders selected on adsorbed proteins cannot bind the soluble conformationoftheantigen. Anotherpossibilityistousecovalentlybindthe antigen to a solid surface using a chemistry reactive on accessible lysine at the surface of the protein of interest, such as the epoxy group[17]. Byavoiding theadsorption process, thisapproachhas the potential to select binders able to bind the native antigen conformation. Finallyanalternativeconsistsinusingabiotinylated versionoftheantigenfortheselection[18].Thisapproachhasthe advantage to allow an interaction between the binders and the antigeninsolutionandatpreciseantigenconcentration. Chapter 10

Selection of Antibodies to Transiently Expressed Membrane Proteins Using Phage Display Martina L. Jones, Stephen M. Mahler, and Sumukh Kumble Abstract Cell membrane proteins serve as attractive targets for biopharmaceutical development in addition to gaugingtheirfundamentalprocessinabiologicalsystem. Approximately38%oftheentiregenomecodes forplasmamembraneproteins;howeverthediscoveryanddevelopmentofantibodybinderstosuchtargets areatechnicalchallenge. Methodstoraisebindersagainstsuchtargetsbycloningandexpressingsoluble extracellular regions have been met with limited success due to the loss of critical epitopes, with the resultingantibodiesfailingtobindtotheirtargetinitsnativeconformation. Thischapteroutlinesa“cell based biopanning” method in order to isolate antibodies against membrane proteins in their native conformationusingtransientlyexpressed, GFP-taggedtargetproteins. Thismethodovercomesthelimitationsofnon-specificbindingofphagetothecells, abundanceofirrelevantantigensonthecellsurface, while retainingthenativestructureoftheantigenonthecellsurface. Keywords Cell-basedbiopanning, Transienttransfection, Phage, Cellsorting, CHOcells, HEK293 cells, Greenfluorescentprotein, Membraneprotein 1 Introduction Integralmembraneproteinsprovideanumberofcriticalbiological functions such as cell osmolarity regulation, cell-to-cell adhesion, and signal transduction [1]. Indeed, membrane proteins are of particular interestas researchersarefocusedonfully dissectingthe biological activity of various cell types, for example, clustered differentiation markers on the surface of immune cells [2]. During pathological events, membrane proteins can be overexpressed in many diseases such as cancer and autoimmunity. As these proteins account for roughly 60% of all drug targets, there is significant research interest in membrane proteins as druggable targets [3]. As such, antibodies against integral membrane proteins are highly desired, both as research reagents and as diagnostic and therapeutic agents. For antibody isolation, both by in vivo immunizationstrategiesandusinginvitrodisplaylibraries, itisnecessary

180 MartinaL.Jonesetal. to present the membrane protein in its correct conformational form. However, theexpressionandpurificationofmembraneproteins are significant technical challenges due to the hydrophobic nature of these molecules. Various attempts have been made, whereby the hydrophilic regions have been cloned and expressed inordertoscreencombinatorialphage-displayedantibodylibraries; howeverthishasledtothedevelopmentofleadcandidatesthatno longer recognize the protein in native biological sources. This can be attributed to the destruction of critical epitopes when the proteinofinterestisimmobilizedontosolidsupportmediumssuchas ELISA plates. An alternative approach involves directly screening cell lines that express the target antigen of interest to ensure the targetisexpressedinitsnativeconformationaccompaniedwiththe appropriate translational modifications such as glycosylation or phosphorylation [4]. Indeed, a number of reports have been published on the successful outcomes of such approaches [5–13]. There are circumstances, however, where the protein of interest may be expressed at low density on the cell surface, which in turn may be obscured by the presence of other endogenous proteins that are present at high levels. In addition, M13 phage particles used for phage display have the propensity to bind non-specifically to the cell surface through phage coat proteins, thus leading to the enrichment of binders that lack antibody expression[14]. Theprotocoldescribedinthischapteraddressesthesetechnical obstacles. In thisprocedure, a construct isgenerated, wherebythe membrane protein of interest is attached to a fluorescent protein such as GFPthat allows for high density expression on the surface of mammalian cells. Transfection of the plasmid construct is then conducted using conventional methods as described by Codamo etal.[15].Theprotocolalsoswitchesthemammalianhostcellline between each round of biopanning to deplete the phage library of irrelevant binders. The biopanning process also involves a low pH wash, wherebythenon-specificbindingofphagetothecellsurface canberemoved[14]followedbysortingofhighlyfluorescentcells, which correlates with antigen expression to enrich for target-specific binders. This method has been successfully utilized in raising antibodies against three membrane proteins [4] and is described in greater detail in this chapter. Selection of Antibody Fragments Against Structured DNA by Phage Display Mahdi Zeraati, Marcel E. Dinger, and Daniel Christ Abstract InadditiontothecanonicalB-formstructure, DNAcanadoptalternativeconformationsincludingZDNA, triplexDNA, aswellasG4andi-Motifquadruplexstructures.Suchstructureshavebeenshowntoformin cellsinadynamicmanner. Monoclonalantibodiesagainstsuchstructuresrepresentkeytoolstostudythe biological functions of these structures. Here we provide protocols for the generation of antibody fragmentsagainststructuredDNAusingphagedisplayselections. Keywords StructuredDNA, Secondarystructure, G-quadruplex, i-Motif, Antibodyfragment, Phage display 1 Introduction In the cell, DNA is predominantly observed in a right-handed double-helical conformation characterized by Watson-Crick base pairing (B-form DNA); this conformation is highly stable under physiologicalconditions[1].However, duringbiologicalprocesses such as replication and transcription, B-form DNA is unwound, allowing for alternative base pairing and the formation of non-B DNA structures [2]. Examples of such DNA structures include Z DNA [3], triplex DNA [4], G-quadruplex (G4) [5], and i-Motif [6]structures(seeFig.1). Based on the results of biophysical and biochemical experiments, severalalgorithmshavebeendevelopedtopredictsequences thatformnon-BDNAstructureswithinthegenome.SuchcomputationalanalysesindicatethatstructuredDNAsarepresentinregulatory regions including promoters, untranslated regions of mRNAs, and telomeres, supporting the notion that non-B DNA structures carry out regulatory functions [7–9]. Consequently, genomic disorders, such as mutations that alter the stability and conformation of these structures, could affect their regulatory function[10,11].Inaddition, stabilizingsuchstructuresthrough

Small molecule ligands that differentiatealternative structured DNA from B-form DNA have been generated for research and therapeutic purposes [14, 15]. Alternatively, monoclonal antibodieshavebeendevelopedtotargetDNAstructuresand aregenerallycharacterizedbyhigherlevelsofaffinityandspecificityfortheir target [16–18]. Those colons can be reproduced in a larger scalefor furthercharacterization. 4 Notes 1. Choosing the right buffer condition is crucial to form the desired non-B DNA structure. It is likely that a unique sequence of oligonucleotide adopts diverse conformation in different buffer conditions. For instance, d[AG (T AG ) ] 3 2 3 3 forms a parallel G-quadruplex in a K+ containing buffer (PDB ID: 1KF1) [5], whereas it adopts antiparallel conformation when K+ is replaced by Na+ in the buffer (PDB ID: 143D) [25]. Therefore, it is recommended to carefully determine appropriate buffer condition for the desired structure and conformation. 2. For bacterial cell cultures, OD of 1.0 ¼ 8 108 cells/ 600 nm mL. Therefore, there are 2 1011 bacterial cells in 500 mL cultureatOD ~0.5.Itisrecommendedtoaddtentimes 600nm moreKM13helperphagestotheculture, inordertomakesure mostofthebacterialcellsgetinfectedbyphages.

With an input of 1012 phages, obtaining approximately 105–107 bacterial colonies after the first and second round of selection is expected. Figures outside this range imply that blocking, washing, and elution conditions are not optimalandneedtobecarefullychecked. Anescalationintiters to 107–109 after three to four rounds of selections usually indicatestheenrichmentofspecificbinders. 6. Following strategies might be implemented to enrich the spe- cificbindersduringsubsequentroundsofselection: (a) AlternatingneutravidinandstreptavidinforcoatingMaxiSorpplates. (b) Decreasing the concentration of DNA target by half for eachsubsequentroundofselection. (c) Increasingthestringencyofwashingstepbydoublingthe number of washing for each subsequent round of selection. (d) Counter-selection against other DNA structures. For example, if selecting for a parallel propeller G-quadruplex structure, phage should be first incubated withacloselyrelatedDNAstructuresuchasanantiparallel G-quadrupleximmobilizedonaMaxiSorpplatefor1hat room temperature and then unbound phages are pooled andusedforselectingagainstthetargetDNAwithdesired conformation. 7. Chapter 12

Selection of Antibody Fragments by Yeast Display Nathalie Scholler Abstract Thecriticalneedforrenewable, high-qualityaffinityreagentsinbiologicalresearch, aswellasfordiagnostic andtherapeuticapplications, hasrequiredthedevelopmentofnewplatformsofdiscovery. Yeastdisplayis oneofthemainmethodsofinvitrodisplaytechnologywithphagedisplay. Yeastdisplayhasbeenchosenby numerousgroupstorefinebothaffinityandspecificityofantibodiesbecauseitenablesfinediscrimination between mutant clones of similar affinity. In addition, the construction of display libraries of antibody fragments inyeast permits tosamplethe immune antibodyrepertoiremorefullythanusing phage. This chaptergivesanupdatedoverviewoftheavailablesystemsofyeastdisplayplatformsandlibraries, followed upbytechnicaldescriptionsofselectionmethodsofantibodyfragmentsbyyeastdisplay. Key words Yeast display scFv libraries, pYD, pAGA2, Magnetic sorting, Flow sorting, Panning, Homologousrecombination, p416BCCP 1 Introduction Hybridomatechnologyhasreliablyprovidedmonoclonalantibody reagents for the past 40 years. Yet, this technology is ridden by inherent limitations such as the dependence on animal immunization and thus could not achieve in vivo generation of antibodies againstlethaltoxinsorpathogens, tolerogenicmolecules, ortargets retained in secretory pathways. In contrast, the use of in vitro display technologies enables the identification of such affinity reagents (for reviews, see [1–4]). For example, recombinant antibodies (scFv) binding to the envelope protein of West Nile virus were identified by yeast display [5, 6], as well as antibodies recognizingallfourserotypesofbotulinumneurotoxinsforrapiddetection in clinical samples [7]. Yeast can be used not only to display proteins, peptides, allergens[8],enzymes[9–11],andevenglycans [12–14] but also to display na¨ıve [15], immunized [16, 17], or synthetic repertoires of various affinity reagents that belong to the superfamily of immunoglobulins or that present alternative scaffolds such as knottins [18], fibronectin 10th type III domain

212 NathalieScholler [19–21],humankringledomainvariants[22,23],orSso7dprotein variants[24,25]. Theyeastdisplaymethodwasfirstdescribedin1997byBoder and Wittrup [26]. The unique capability of this approach for very fine discrimination between mutant clones of similar affinity became rapidly evident [27]. Because fine discrimination is critical for rapid assessment of affinity maturation, the selection of antibody fragments by yeast display has been chosen by numerous groups to refine both affinity and specificity. Superior quality of reagentswasobtained, evenfordifficulttargetssuchassmallmolecules (haptens), including fluorescein for which Boder and colleagues isolated antibody fragments with a monovalent antigen-binding affinity of 48fM [28]. Yeast display platform was also showntobeusefulfortheidentificationofaffinityreagentsbinding to inorganic material surfaces, enabling the study of mechanisms governing interfacial interactions and the generation of materialspecificreagents[29].Furthermore, thedirectcomparisonofyeast and phage display using the same scFv cDNA library derived from HIV-1 immune patients, and screened by the same selecting antigen (HIV-1 gp120), demonstrated that yeast display sampled the immuneantibodyrepertoiremorefullythanphagedisplay[30]. Yeast display has been trusted by many groups to improve the affinityandspecificityofrecognitionreagentsandbecamealeading platform for protein engineering [31, 32]. Simple methods for creating diversity are based on the amplification by error-prone PCR or on the use of an E. coli mutator strain to mutagenize an antibody fragment [26, 33]. Such methods have improved the affinity of scFv variants for TCR [34] and of Fab up to 10-fold after selection by flow cytometry analysis [35], with an increase of potency of 238-fold for a bivalent immunotoxin scFv [36]. However, to increase the specificity by several hundred folds, directed evolution is required (for review, see [37]). The yeast display method also facilitates directed evolution as shown by various groups, including by Shusta and colleagues who evolved single-chain T cell receptors (scTCR) to enhance stability and soluble expression, which correlated with improved resistance to thermal denaturation and intracellular processing [38], Weaver-Feldhaus and colleagues who reported an increase of specificity of more than300-foldforasingle-domain(VH)clonedirectedtocalmodulin[39],andOrcuttetal.whopublishedanincreaseofspecificity of1000-foldforaDOTA-chelate-bindingscFv[40].Directedevolutionhasalsobeenusedtoengineerstabilizedvariantsofasinglechain form of the class II region of the major histocompatibility complex(MHC)I-A(g7)[41]. While there are multiple options for anchoring proteins at the yeastcellsurface, suchasGPI-anchoredproteins(Cwp1p,Cwp2p, Tip1p, Tir1/Sed1p) or flocculin Flo1p (review in [42]), the first published system of yeast display based on mating type-specific

SelectionofAntibodyFragmentsbyYeastDisplay 213 agglutinins (Agα1p and Aga2p) remains the most widely used. Aga2 receptor stabilizes cell-cell interactions and facilitates fusion betweenmating“a”and αhaploidyeastcells.a-Agglutininsystem is composed of a core subunit encoded by AGA1 (Agα1) that is linked to a small binding subunit encoded by AGA2 (Aga2) by disulfide bonds during secretion. After secretion, Agα1 attaches covalentlyto b-glucanofthe yeastcellwall. Thefusion ofAga2 in N-terminal of the protein fragment of interest permits protein display at the yeast cell surface [26]. The fusion to Aga2 has also been used to display transient or unstable complexes that can dissociate during a long induction. The “STUCKED” method, stabilization of transient and unstable complexes by engineered disulfide, wasdevelopedtocost-andtime-effectivelystudyquaternary structures. The protein complex, including scFv, is displayed on the yeast surface as described in [43], with one subunit expressed as a fusion with Aga2 and the other one expressed as a soluble form. A cysteine residue is introduced in each subunit to formanintersubunitdisulfide. Theengineeredinterchaindisulfide helps stabilizing the protein complex [44]. The same principle of yeast display has also been used to create very large combinatorial Fablibrariesbymating.Todoso, Weaver-Feldhausandcolleagues amplifiedtheheavy(V )andfirstconstantregions(CH1)aswellas H the variable light chains (Vκ) from B cells of non-immunized donors. The constant light chain was amplified from the C gene k (accession number P01834). Cloning by homologous recombination was performed by co-transformation of YVH10 yeast strain with Vκ fragments and the linearized vector pPNL30 for yeast secretion; pPNL30 was derived from pPNL9 after the addition of C. Similarly, JAR300, the mating partner of YVH10, was k co-transformed with V fragments and linearized vector pPNL20 H for yeast display, derived from pCTcon after the addition of CH1. Although the transformation yields were relatively modest, the yeastmating ofYVH10secretingV +C with JAR300displaying k k V +CH1couldgenerateaverylargelibraryofdisplayedFab[43]. H YeastdisplayvectorsbasedonAga2-Agα1interactionareavailable.pYDvectorhasbeenwidelyused, includingfor thedisplayof nanobodies (VHH) [45] that are functional antibodies devoid of light chains, found incamelids(Bactriancamels, dromedaries, and llamas) [46] and in some cartilaginous fish [47]. These singledomainantibodiesbindantigenswithoutrequiringdomainpairing and are remarkably resistant against extreme pH and chaotropic agents, makingthemespeciallysuitedfororalimmunotherapy(for review, see [48]). The pYD vector has been further modified by several groups. For example, Wang and colleagues modified the fusionsideofAga2toscFvinpYD1andreportedthatthefusionof Aga2inC-terminusofthescFvusingtheirnewvectorcalledpYD5 improvestheexpressionofsomescFv[49].VandenBeuckenetal. havereengineeredpYD1tomakeitsuitableforFabexpression, by

214 NathalieScholler adaptingtoyeastasthemostfrequentlyusedformatforFabdisplay onphage[50].TheresultingpTQ3vectorcontainstwoexpression cassettes driven by identical inducible promoters, one for each variable chain, and enables display and affinity maturation of heterodimeric Fab antibodies. The tandem expression on S. cerevisiae surface of the variable heavy chain (V ) fused to Aga2 and of the H solublelightchain(V )isgalactose-driven[35]. L Novelantibody-relatedstructuressuchaslampreyvariablelymphocytereceptors(VLRs)andAdnectins, anewfamilyoftherapeutic proteins based on the 10th fibronectin type III domain [51], havealsobeendisplayedonyeast. ThedisplayofaVLRlibrarywas achieved through fusion to the yeast Flo 1p surface anchor [52]. While phage display of major histocompatibility complex proteins (MHC) has proven to be extremely challenging, yeast display enabled assembly and display of MHC heterodimers with entirely noncovalent interchain interactions. But, although yeast displayMHCcouldbindtopeptides, theywerenotabletostimulate antigen-specific T cells [53], and efforts in understanding MHC functional structure and stabilization are still ongoing [54]. Yeast surface display of T cell receptor (TCR) using pYD was undertaken usingthree or two TCR domains, Vα, Vβ, and Cβ (scTCR) or Vα linked to Vβ (scTv), respectively. Stabilization of yeast display scTv could be achieved by mutating the interface of the Vα and Vβ chains and the Vβ-chain framework region [55], while the addition of a disulfide bond allowed stable display of scTCRonyeast[56]. Limitationshavebeenreportedregardingthedisplayofheterologous proteins on S. cerevisiae, including N-linked glycosylation and, toalesserextent, coredisulfides[57].Severalalternativeplatforms for yeast display on S. cerevisiae and on Pichia pastoris have been developed. Alternative yeast display strategies of antibody fragments on S. cerevisiae include the co-expression of the scFv fusedtotheadapterGR1andofthegeneticallyintegratedadapter GR2 fused to the outer wall protein Cwp2, which permits the pairwise interaction of the scFv-GR1 and GR2-Cwp2 fusions in the yeast cells resulting in scFv display [58], and the use of the classical streptavidin/biotin interaction to display in vivo biotinylatedantibodies[59]atavidinatedyeastcellsurface[Secretionand CaptureTechnology(SECANT)platform][60]. Finally, tools for display on Pichia pastoris, a yeast strain that compares favorably to S. cerevisiae in terms of yield and of posttranslationalmodifications[61,62],havebeenrecentlydeveloped. Jacobs et al. first adapted the Aga2-based display technology in P. pastoris [63]. Later, Su and colleagues used the Sed1 anchor system under the control of the alcohol oxidase 1 promoter (pAOX1) to display Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB) and obtained large amounts of hydrolytic activity of the displayed CALB (more than 220 U/g dry cells after 120 h of culture)

SelectionofAntibodyFragmentsbyYeastDisplay 215 [64]. In the same year, Rychaert et al. fused an immune library of camelid nanobodies directed against green fluorescence protein to the C-terminal part of the S. cerevisiae alpha-agglutinin gene (SAG1) for display on P. pastoris [65]. Finally, in 2011 Jo et al. publishedtheuseofthegeneTIP1encodingtheglycosylphosphatidylinositol(GPI)-anchoredproteinofS.cerevisiaeasananchoring motiftofusetohumanlactoferrincDNA(hLf).ThefusedhLFwas biologically active at the surface of P. pastoris, as demonstrated by the antibacterial activity of the intact recombinant yeast cells and celllysatesagainsttargetmicroorganisms[66]. These examples underline the remarkable potential of yeast display technology for a wide range of applications. However, phage display is often preferred to yeast display as a method of antibody selection. This bias in favor of phage is probably based in part on habits, as the yeast display platform appeared more recently [26] than the phage display one [67]. But the lack of yeast sorting expertise and of adequate equipment, as well as the low transformation efficiency of yeast to compare with bacteria, may also have played an important role (for review, see [68]). The goal of this chapter is to give an updated overview of the available systemsofyeastdisplaylibrariesofantibodyfragmentsandvectors, followed up by technical advices to make more accessible to the generaluser theselectionofantibodyfragmentsbyyeastdisplay. 2 Materials 1. Rapid Selection of High-Affinity Antibody scFv Fragments Using Ribosome Display Birgit Dreier and Andreas Plu¨ckthun Abstract Ribosomedisplayhasproventobeapowerfulinvitroselectionandevolutionmethodforgeneratinghighaffinity binders from libraries of folded proteins. It works entirely in vitro, and this has two important consequences. First, sincenotransformationofanycellsisrequired, librarieswithmuchgreaterdiversity canbehandledthanwithmostother techniques. Second, sincealibrarydoesnothavetobeclonedand transformed, itisveryconvenienttointroducerandomerrorsinthelibrarybyPCR-basedmethodsand selectimprovedbinders. Thus, atruedirectedevolution, aniterationbetweenrandomizationandselection over several generations, can be conveniently carried out, e.g., for affinity maturation, either on a given cloneoronthewholelibrary. Ribosomedisplayhasbeensuccessfullyappliedtoantibodysingle-chainFv fragments(scFv),whichcanbeselectednotonlyforspecificitybutalsoforstabilityandcatalyticactivity. High-affinitybinderswithnewtargetspecificitycanbeobtainedfromhighlydiverselibrariesinonlyafew selectionrounds. Inthisprotocol, theselectionfromthelibraryandtheprocessofaffinitymaturationand off-rateselectionareexplainedindetail. Key words Ribosome display, In vitro selection, In vitro translation, Antibody scFv fragments, Affinitymaturation 1 Introduction Ribosome display is a potent in vitro method to select and evolve proteinsorpeptidesfromana¨ıvelibrarywithveryhighdiversityto bind to any chosen target of interest [1–6]. No cells need to be transformedwiththelibrary, andthusthefullavailablediversitycan be subjected to selection, and not only the aliquot that ends up in transformedcells, likeinmostotherdisplaymethods. Akeyfeature of ribosome display, in contradistinction to most other selection technologies[6],isthatitincorporatesPCRintotheprocedureand thus allows a convenient incorporation of a diversification (“randomization”) step. Thereby, ribosome display allows refinement andaffinitymaturationnotonlyofpreexistingbinders, eitherindividual or combined to a small collection [7–12], but also of the

236 BirgitDreierandAndreasPlu¨ckthun whole pool directly during selection from a complex library, if desired. This is one of the major advantages of ribosome display overotherselectionstrategies. Thediversityofthelibrarymembers can be easily manipulated at any selection step by introduction of additional mutations, e.g., by using DNA shuffling [13] and/or error-prone PCR [14], as has been done in the above examples. Thisadditionalrandomizationstepcanreadilybeintegratedinthe protocol(seeSubheadings3.11.1and3.11.2).Incombinationwith off-rate selection (see Subheading 3.11.3) where binders to the biotinylated target protein are competed with a molar excess of non-biotinylated target protein, many initial leads were improved foraffinityintherangeoflownMtolowpM[3,7,9–11,15].The theoretical considerations for designing efficient off-rate selection experimentshavebeensummarizedelsewhere[16]. Wehaveoriginallydevelopedtheribosomedisplayprotocolfor antibodyscFvfragments[5,8,17].Wehaveapplieditinthedirect selectionfromlibraries[1,3,17],whereitcombinesselectionwith affinity maturation, and in the evolution of single clones [9, 15, 18]. Most antibody fragments require disulfide bonds for proper folding, and thus, it was initially a concern, whether ribosome display mightonly befeasiblefor the subsetof antibodiesthat can fold without proper disulfide formation. To answer this question, experimentshadbeencarriedoutpriortodevelopingtheribosome display protocol for antibodies, in order to investigate native foldingofantibodyscFvfragmentsduringinvitrotranslation[19].The key conclusion was that disulfide isomerization is indeed very important but can be efficiently catalyzed by eukaryotic protein disulfide isomerase (PDI). This finding was the key reason whyinourribosomedisplayprotocolstranscriptionandtranslation are not coupled: transcription can thus be run in the presence of DTT, translation(andfolding)initsabsence. Occasionally, ithasbeensurmisedthateukaryoticproteinssuch as antibody fragments should be better produced in vitro by eukaryotic ribosomes than prokaryotic ones. However, a direct comparisongavenoevidencefor thisbelief[20]. In recent years we have extended the in vitro selection to protein scaffolds with more favorable biophysical properties than antibodyfragments, theDesignedAnkyrinRepeatProteins(DAR- Pins) [21, 22]. DARPins, which aredevoid of disulfide bonds, are highlysolubleandhighlystableandthereforeachievehighexpression levels in E. coli [23] and have thus been found versatile tools formanyapplicationsinlaboratoryresearch, diagnostics, andtherapy [22]. They also fold well in the in vitro translation inherent in ribosomedisplayandarethusreadilyenrichedforbindingspecificity. Using ribosome display, DARPins have been evolved to bind various targets with affinities all the way down to the picomolar range [7, 10, 24–32]. A protocol describing their selection has beenpublished.

RibosomeDisplaySelectionofscFvFragments 237 Some applications using antibody fragments, e.g., for therapy, requirehighstabilityofthetherapeuticagent[33–35].Selectionfor high stability can also be achieved with display technologies [18, 36–38]. If thestabilityisalready highbutanevenmore stable molecule is desired, this can be achieved by first making the whole populationunabletofoldbyintroducingareversibledestabilization, andthenselectingforcompensatingmutations, andfinallyremoving the destabilization again. For example, most antibody domains require disulfides for stability, which form only under oxidizing conditions. A destabilization and increase in aggregation of the antibody fold is usually observed when the disulfides are removed [39, 40]. Using a reducing environment during the selection, scFv antibody fragments could be evolved that were able to fold under reducing conditions correlating with conditions in the cytosol, and they showed higher stability than the starting molecule in the absence of the disulfide bonds [18] but also after the disulfide bonds were allowed to form again. Antibody fragments with these improved biophysical property can be used in biomedical applications with disulfides formed, but they also make an intracellular application(as“intrabodies”)[41]morefeasible. Inaddition, rational design of the antibody framework [42] could contribute to the developmentofstability-improved, antibody-basedtherapeutics. Wereporthere the most recent version ofthe standard protocols for selection from a complex library and affinity maturation usingoff-rateselection. Theperiplasmicexpressionandpurification of scFv fragments of antibodies is not covered in this chapter but has been described elsewhere [43, 44]. Fig. 1 Scheme of the ribosome display cycle. In ribosome display all steps of the selection are performed in vitro. The cycle begins with a DNA library (top) in the form of a PCR fragment encoding a library of the proteinofinterestandcontainingaT7promoterandribosome-bindingsite. TheORFofinterest(lightgray)is fusedtoanadditionalproteinregion(the“spacer”or“tether,”checkeredwhite).Thistetherorspacer, here used as an unstructured region from the CT domain of geneIII from filamentous phage M13, has the sole function of allowing the protein domain of interest to emerge from the ribosomal tunnel. Therefore, any non-globularpolarproteinsequencecaninprinciplebeused.APCRisthencarriedoutfromthepromoterto the middle of the tether. Importantly, the PCR fragment does not encode a stop codon at the end. Each member of the library pool is then transcribed from double-stranded DNA into mRNA and is subsequently translated by the ribosomes present in an E. coli S30 extract, leading to ternary complexes consisting of ribosomes, mRNA, andthescFvfragmentsencodedbythatparticularmRNA.Sincethereisnostopcodonon themRNA, theproteinisnotreleased fromtheribosome. Itisbelievedtobestillcovalently attached tothe tRNAwithintheribosome, withthetetherinthetunnel, andthedomainofinterestoutsideandalreadyfolded. Selection can be achieved by binding the protein-ribosome-mRNA complexes to the desired immobilized target, followedbyremovalofunboundornon-specificallyboundproteinbystringentwashing. Affinitycanbe increased by addition of an excess of non-labeled target (off-rate selection) (see Subheading 3.11.3). Particular selectivity in binding can be achieved by adding an unwanted target as a competitor. Selection for other properties, such as stability, requires other selection pressures at this step [18, 34, 39, 41, 42]. Binders can be easily recovered by destruction of the protein-ribosome-mRNA complex using EDTA and recovery of the genetic information of the binders by RT-PCR using the primer set SDA and T3Te. The initialproductisthenamplifiedusingprimersT7BandT3TetointroducetheT7promotersequenceandpartof thestabilizing50stemloop.TheT3TeprimerbindsinthesequenceofthegeneIIIspacerregionandintroduces astabilizing30stemloop.Iffurtherdiversityisrequired, anerror-pronePCRcanbeincludedatthisstep.The amplifiedPCRproductthenservesastemplateforinvitrotranscription, initiatingthenextroundofselection.

Usually after the third round of ribosome display, the PCR scFvs products are cloned into a vector, and E. coli are transformed, such that the binding specificity of single clones can be evaluated by ELISA. There are three principal strategies for achieving this. The primers chosen for the last PCR amplification shouldcommensuratewiththedestinationvector: (a) Since antibody scFv fragments carry disulfide bonds, which are required for correct folding, it is best to clone the scFv genes into a secretion vector behind a bacterial signal sequence. The vector pAK400 [52, 53] allows directional cloning via two SfiI sites with different overhangs (Fig. 3) and leads to strong expression. This strategyshouldnormallybechosenfirst. (b) The genes can alternatively be cloned into the vector pTFT74 [43] via NcoI and HindIII (Figs. 2b and 3). This vector does not contain a signal sequence and will express the genes under control of the T7 promoter. Thus, after plasmid minipreps, the antibody scFv gene can be translated in vitro in the presence of disulfide isomerase [19]. This strategy will of course yield much lessproteinthanthedirectexpressionfromE.colibutcan beveryvaluableintroubleshooting, astheinvitrofolding conditionswillbeverysimilarasintheribosomeselection itself. (c) Finally, usingthesamevector, pTFT7443,the protein can be produced from E. coli, albeit as inclusion bodies which have to be refolded [17, 43]. This is not practicalforaverylargenumberofsamplesbutcansometimesprovidelargeamountsofaparticularscFvfragment veryrapidly. (d) Wecannotgiveafullaccountofantibodyexpressionhere. Perform one cycle of non-stringent selection including an error-prone PCR followed by a round of off-rate selection without error-prone PCR. The rationale is that error-prone PCR will generate many nonfunctional molecules. First, all functional molecules should be recovered by a non-stringent selection, and then from this pool of functional (randomized) molecules, thebestonesshouldberecovered. Forthispurpose perform a stringent round using off-rate selection. After this stringent round, the number of remaining functional molecules, most of them of very high-affinity, can be very low, such that background binding becomes an issue. Thus, the nonselective round will simply amplify these functional, highaffinitymolecules. 23. Here are some general considerations [16]: subsequent selec- tion rounds with modest selection pressure (“recovery rounds”) are recommended to follow after high-stringency selection rounds, because this will lead to higher diversity. Start at 10- to 100-fold excess competitor; increase to 100to 10,000-fold in later rounds, if feasible. In Vitro Selection of Single-Domain Antibody (VHH) Using cDNA Display Naoto Nemoto, Shigefumi Kumachi, and Hidenao Arai Abstract Single-domain antibody (e.g., Nanobody, VHH antibody) is a promising scaffold for therapeutic and diagnostic reagents. To expand the range of target molecules, in vitro selection using cell-free display technologiessuchascDNAdisplayisusefulandpowerfulbecauseoftheirhugelibrariesandrobuststability. Weprovidetechnicaldetailsforinvitroselectionofsingle-domainantibodiesusingcDNAdisplay. Keywords cDNAdisplay, mRNAdisplay, Invitroselection, Nanobody, VHH, Cell-freetranslation, Puromycin, Evolutionarymolecularengineering, Directedevolution, Proteinengineering, Antibody engineering 1 Introduction Genotype-phenotype linking technologies such as phage display have been widely applied for selection of functional peptides and proteins. Recently, invitrodisplaytechnologiesthatareusedwitha cell-free translation system have become more promising because (~1013) of their huge library size and incorporation of nonnatural amino acids to peptides [1]. cDNA display is a new version of mRNA display that is one of the simplest genotype-phenotype linking methods [2–7] (Fig. 1a). cDNA display is more stable than other in vitro display methods because cDNA is fused to its codingpolypeptide covalently viaapuromycin molecule[8, 9].In addition, the preparation of cDNA display molecules is very easy with cnvK-linker (Fig. 1b), which is capable of being linked with mRNA covalently by UV radiation (360 nm) after hybridization [10].Inthischapter, weintroducehowcDNAdisplayisappliedfor selection of VHH antibody (nanobody). VHH libraries can be prepared by DNA synthesizer as well as from na¨ıve libraries from Camillidaeanimals[11,12].Inthefollowingprotocol, weassume thatthelibrarywasgiven.

276 NaotoNemotoetal. 3 Methods Schematic representation of cDNA display method for the screening from a VHH library is shown in Fig. 3. (1) The DNA library

encoding VHH is transcribed into mRNAs. (2) The mRNA is ligated by UV irradiation with the puromycin-linker to form the mRNA-linkerfusionmolecule.(3)ThemRNA-linkerfusionmolecule is translated to synthesize mRNA-linker-VHH fusion molecules(termedas“mRNAdisplay”molecules)andareimmobilized onto SA magnetic beads. (4) The mRNA moiety of the immobilized mRNA display molecules is reverse-transcribed to synthesize the mRNA-/cDNA-linker-VHH fusion molecule (termed as “cDNAdisplay”molecule).ThecDNAdisplaymoleculeisreleased fromSAbeadsbytreatmentwithRNaseT1.(5)ThecDNAdisplay moleculeispurifiedusingtheNi-NTAmagneticbeadtoeliminate Fig.3SchematicrepresentationofthecDNAdisplay.TheDNAlibraryencodingVHHistranscriptedintomRNA (Subheading3.2).AnmRNAisphoto-cross-linkedwithPuromycin-linker(subheading3.2).Thecross-linking productisinvitrotranslated(Subheading3.4.1).ThetranslatedmRNA-proteinfusionisimmobilizedontoSA beads forpurification (Subheading3.4.2).The immobilized fusionis reverse transcribedtoform an mRNA-/ cDNA-proteinfusion(cDNAdisplaymolecule)(Subheading3.4.3).ThecDNAdisplaymoleculeisreleasedfrom SAbeadsbyRNaseT1digestion(Subheading3.4.4)andpurifiedbyHis-tagpurification(Subheading3.4.4). ThepurifiedcDNAdisplay, whichbindstoimmobilizedtargetmolecule, isamplifiedbyPCR(Subheadings3.6 and3.7),andfullconstructDNAispreparedbyoverlapextensionforthenextscreeningcycleorcloning

InVitroSelectionofSingle-DomainAntibody(VHH)UsingcDNADisplay 277 the mRNA-linker fusion molecule. (6) The processed cDNA display molecule is incubated with the target molecule, which is immobilized on a resin or bead (see Note 7). (7) The bound cDNA display molecule is collected and amplified by PCR for the next round of in vitro selection. Chapter 15

Sequencing and Affinity Determination of Antigen-Specific B Lymphocytes from Peripheral Blood Peter Schofield, Rodrigo Vazquez-Lombardi, Mahmoud Abdelatti, Damien Nevoltris, Christopher C. Goodnow, Daniel Christ, and Joanne H. Reed Abstract Here we describe methods for screening human blood to isolate peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) capable of binding fluorescently labeled antigen, as well as methods for the amplification and sequencing of B cell receptor (BCR) heavy and light chain genes. Detailed protocols are provided for transientmammalianexpressioninahexahistidine-taggedFabformat, purificationbyimmobilizedmetal affinitychromatography(IMAC),andaffinitydeterminationbyBioLayerinterferometry(BLI). Keywords Bcell receptor, Single-cell sequencing, Antigen-specific Bcells, Mammalian expression, Affinitydetermination 1 Introduction 1.1 ScreeningBlood Common techniques used for the isolation of antigen-specific B forAntigen-SpecificB cells include capturing B cells on a solid support coated with an CellsandSequencing antigenofinterestoraddingfluorescentlyconjugatedsolubleantiofBCellReceptor gendirectlytoBcellsforflowcytometry-basedsorting[1].Theuse Genes of flow cytometry single-cell sorting is particularly advantageous becausethisapproachmaintainsthenaturalimmunoglobulinheavy and light chain gene pairing [2]. This technique also enables sampling of various B cell developmental stages to track antibody evolution [3, 4] and allows for the determination of full length heavy and light chain sequences for biotechnology applications [5, 6]. The steps outlined below assume that a purified protein with a size of at least 10 kDa is used as an antigen. For protein antigens less than 10 kDa, and for other small molecule targets (such as haptens), coupling to carrier protein such as ovalbumin (OVA),bovineserumalbumin(BSA),orkeyholelimpethemocyanin(KLH)isrecommended.

Until recently, a major ofAntigen-SpecificB disadvantage of transient expression in mammalian cells was rela- CellReceptorsasFab tivelylowyields, mainlyduetoavailablesurfacearealimitingadher- Fragments ent cell growth [7]. Initially limited to biopharmaceutical companies, suspension-adaptedandserum-freemammalianexpressionsystems, asoutlinedhere, arenowmorebroadlyavailable. Such systems are capable of supporting high cell densities (> 1 107 cells/mL), which in conjunction with the use of transcriptional enhancers leads to improved expression yields ranging from tens tohundredsofmilligramsperliterofculture[8,9]. The current protocol describes expression in a hexahistidinetagged Fab format (V C 1/V C ). Titration of antibodies on human PBMCs is recommended prior to sorting to obtain the optimal concentration of antibody. Titration experiments should be performed using the same staining conditions and density of cells as recommended for theexperiment(20106cells/mL),e.g.,1106cellsin 50 μL final volume. For most commercially available human antibodies, astartingdilutionof1/20isrecommendedwitha twofoldserialdilutionof5–8points.Pancellmarkerantibodies (e.g., CD19, CD3) should be titrated as a single stain. Antibodies specific for low-frequency populations (e.g., CD10) should be titrated in the presence of pan marker antibodies. Thefluorescentlylabeledantigenshouldalsobetitrated, inthe presence of the complete stain, to obtain the optimal concentration for staining. Optimal concentrations are where the highest saturating signal is obtained on positive populations (e.g.,CD19+Bcells)withthelowestsignalonnegativepopulations(e.g.,CD3+Tcells). 6. The B cell stain should be evaluated in conjunction with the fluorescently labeled antigen by flow cytometry prior to sorting. Usingthe gating strategy shown in Fig. 1, we can calculate that the antigen-specific B cells are 0.3% of total B cells, which are 10.2% of lymphocytes (45.8% of the Ficoll-histopaque PBMC preparation). Therefore, to obtain one 96-well plate of antigen-specific B cells, approximately 7.0 105 PBMC (~3.3 104 B cells) would be required as starting material. Part IV

Production of Recombinant Antibodies

Chapter 16

Expression of IgG Monoclonals with Engineered Immune Effector Functions Rodrigo Vazquez-Lombardi, Damien Nevoltris, Romain Rouet, and Daniel Christ Abstract The therapeutic development of monoclonal antibodies requires robust and reliable methods for their recombinant expression and characterization. In this context, an increasingly important aspect in the antibodydevelopmentprocessistodeterminethecontributionofFc-mediatedimmuneeffectorfunctions to therapeutic activity. Here we describe steps for the cloning and mammalian expression of mouse and human IgG monoclonals with reduced immune effector functions, based on mutation of Fc-gamma receptor and complement-binding sites. Theresulting antibody preparations containlow levelsofendotoxinandaresuitablefortestinginanimalmodelsofdisease. Keywords Antibodies, ImmunoglobulinG(IgG),Antibodyvariabledomains, Fcregion, Mammalianexpression, Effectorfunctions, Immunotherapy 1 Introduction 1.1 Transient RecombinantexpressionofimmunoglobulinG(IgG)monoclonal ExpressionofIgG antibodiesisanessentialtechniquerequiredfor theirdevelopment Antibodies as therapeutics. Transient recombinant expression is of particular inMammalianCells importanceduringearlystagesofantibodydevelopment, asseveral antibody candidates can be produced and characterized in a relatively short period of time. This is in contrast to stable antibody expression, which supports higher yields but requires significant time and resources for the identification of a suitable antibodyproducingclonalcellline. Transientexpressionofantibodiesandantibodyfragmentshas been traditionally performed in inexpensive bacterial expression systems, particularly in E. coli [1]. However, bacterial antibody expression is associated with a number of shortcomings including lackofantibodyfragmentcrystallizable(Fc)glycosylation[2],low yields(especiallyforfull-lengthIgG)andcontaminationwithpyrogenic endotoxin [3]. These disadvantages are biologically relevant

314 RodrigoVazquez-Lombardietal. asantibodyglycosylationisarequirementforFc-mediatedimmune effector functions (see Subheading 1.2) and contaminating endotoxins may interfere with the interpretation of both in vitro and invivoassays[4–7].Whilealternativeexpressionsystemsbasedon yeast and insect cells can address some of these disadvantages, antibodies produced in such cells display different glycosylation patternstothoseobservedinmammaliancells[8]. Sincethegreat majorityofapprovedtherapeuticantibodiesareproducedinmammaliancells[9],itisdesirabletoimplementmammalianexpression fromearlystagesofdevelopment. Recentadvancesincommercially available transient mammalian expression systems support improved recombinant antibody yields and are consequently becoming more cost-effective [10, 11]. These expression systems allow for the expression of candidate IgG antibodies in milligram quantities, sufficient for initial proof-of-concept experiments in animalmodelsofdisease. 1.2 Antibody Antibody Fc-mediated effector functions can be critical for the MediatedImmune therapeuticactivityofmonoclonalantibodydrugs. Thisisexempli- EffectorFunctions fiedbytheincreasedefficacyoftrastuzumab(anti-HER2)inbreast cancer patients with favorable Fc-gamma receptor (FcγR) polymorphisms [12]. Fc-mediated immune effector functions rely on the interaction between residues in the antibody Fc region and both FcγRs and the complement C1q component. Upon binding acell-surfacetarget, theantibodyFcregionrecruitscellsexpressing FcγRs (e.g. NK cells, monocytes, and macrophages) capable of antibody-dependentcell-mediatedcytotoxicity(ADCC)orphagocytosis (ADCP) of the target cell [13]. In addition, the Fc region servesasadockingsiteforthecomplementcomponentC1q.Once boundtoFc, C1qcaninitiatetheformationofamembraneattack complex (MAC) that functions to lyse the target cell, a process known as complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) [14]. More recently characterized mechanisms that rely on Fc-mediated C1q deposition involve the recruitment of immune cells expressing complement receptors (CRs) for the facilitation of complement-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (CDCC) and phagocytosis (CDCP)[15]. Fc-mediated effector functions can be modulated through antibody engineering for therapeutic purposes. Modulation of Fc-mediatedeffector functionsisanimportantaspectoftherapeuticantibodydevelopment, anditisimportanttodeterminewhether aprimarilyblocking(noeffectorfunctions)oradepleting(effector functions) mode of action is desirable for a specific indication and target. This is clearly exemplified by antibodies targeting immune checkpoint molecules. For monoclonals targeting PD-1, Fc-mediated effector functions are undesirable as these may cause unwanted depletion of tumor-reactive CD8+ Tcells [16]. On the other hand, anti-CTLA-4 antibodies benefit from Fc-mediated

The pRVL expression plasmids contain two SapI restriction sites to allow for variable domain cloning. Endogenous SapI restriction sites present in constant antibody domains have beenremovedtopreventunwantedplasmiddigestion. Accordingly, it is essential to have prior knowledge of the V and V L H gene sequences to be cloned. If using PCR products for cloning, V and V sequences should not contain internal SapI L H restriction sites. If V L and/or V H sequences contain SapI restriction sites, it is possible to remove them in silico and to purchase the gene in question as a synthesized gene fragment (see Note 5). Alternatively, cloning can be performed by gene assemblyusingsuitablydesignedprimers[30]. 5. Custom-designedV andV genefragmentscanbepurchased L H from specialized vendors (e.g., IDT gBlocks). Doing so is particularly useful for V and V sequences derived from L H hybridoma cells or antigen-specific B-cells, as PCR from extracted cDNA may require extensive optimization. Gene fragments should contain no internal SapI restriction sites andcanbedesignedusingthefollowingtable. Dest. An IRES-Mediated Tricistronic Vector for Efficient Generation of Stable, High-Level Monoclonal Antibody Producing CHO DG44 Cell Lines Jessna H. M. Yeo, Mariati, and Yuansheng Yang Abstract The generation of stable, high-level monoclonal antibody (mAb) producing cell lines remains a major challengeinbiopharmaceuticalindustry. ThecommonlyusedplasmidvectorsformAbexpression, which expresslightchain(LC),heavychain(HC),andselectionmarkergenesonseparatevectorsorviamultiple promotersonasinglevector, arenotabletoaccuratelycontroltheratioofLCoverHCexpressionandtend toresultinnon-expressingclones. Toovercometheseissues, wehavedevelopedatricistronicvectorusing two internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) to express the LC, HC, and dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) selectionmarkergenesinonetranscript. Inthistricistronicvector, thethreegenesareunderthecontrolofa hapten-modifiedhumancytomegalovirus(hCMV)promotercontainingacoreCpGislandelement(IE)to enhancetheproductionstability. TheLCgeneisarrangedasthefirstcistronfollowedbyawild-typeIRES tocontroltheHCexpression.SuchdesignexpressesexcessLCpolypeptideswhichenhancemAbexpressionlevelandreduceaggregate.AmutatedIRESwithattenuatedstrengthisappliedonDHFRtoreduceits expressionforenhancingthestringencyofselectionforhighproducers. Thisvectorallowseasygeneration of stable, high mAb producing CHO DG44 pools and clones for antibody development and manufacturing. Keywords CHO, Monoclonalantibody, Tricistronic, IRES, CoreCpGislandelement 1 Introduction Monoclonalantibodies(mAbs)havebeenprovenaseffectivetools for a wide spectrum of research, diagnostic, and therapeutic applications. Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells are the predominant hostforproducingmAbsduetotheircapabilitytoperformproper folding and assembly of complex proteins and posttranslational modifications [1]. There are two major approaches for mAb productioninCHOcells, transienttransfectionandstabletransfection. Theformerapproach allows for rapid production of smallamount of mAbs and is more suitable for applications in biochemical, biophysical, and preclinical studies at early stage of mAb

336 JessnaH.M.Yeoetal. development[2].Thelatterapproachwhichconsistsoftwomajor steps, generationofstablytransfectedpoolsfollowedbyisolationof clones, takes longer time but can produce greater amount of proteins. The high-producing stably transfected pools can be used in preclinical studies which require more proteins that cannot be satisfiedbytransienttransfections[3],whilethesingle-cell-derived clonesarerequiredformanufacturingantibodiesforinvestigational new drug (IND)-enabling toxicology studies, clinical trials, and commercial production [4]. To meet the regulatory and production requirements, the production clones need to have high productivity, good product quality, and long-term stable production. The generation of stable, high-level mAb producing pools and clones remains a major challenge in biopharmaceutical industry. A large number of clones need to be screened for obtaining high productivity and stable production due to the nature of random integrationofplasmidvectorsintothechromosomesandthelarge variationsintheactivityofthenumerousintegrationsites[5–7]. Vectoroptimization isoneof themosteffectiveapproaches to improve the efficiency of cell line development. An IgG mAb moleculecomprisestwoidenticallightchains(LCs)andtwoidentical heavy chains (HCs). The ratio of LC over HC expression affects both mAb expression level and quality [8–16]. The commonlyusedplasmidvectorsformAbexpression, whichexpressLC, HC, and selection marker genes on separate vectors or using a single vector with multiple promoters, are not able to accurately control the ratio of LC over HC expression [6, 9, 15, 17]. In addition, the expression of product and selection genes is not tightlycoupledwhichresultsinmanynon-expressingcellsinstably transfected pools [18, 19]. Another drawback of the commonly usedvectorsformAbexpressionisthattheyusehumancytomegalovirus (hCMV) MIE gene for obtaining high mAb expression levels. This promoter is susceptible to gene silencing during long-term cultures, resulting in unstable production in the majority of clones[6,20–29]. To overcome issues associated with the traditional vectors, we developed a tricistronic vector using two encephalomyocarditis virus (EMCV) internal ribosome entry sites (IRES) to express the LC, HC,andselectionmarkergenesinonetranscript(Fig.1).Such design not only provides precise control of LC: HC ratios in different clones but also minimizes the occurrence of non-expressing clones [9]. To enhance production stability, we used a modified human cytomegalovirus promoter (CMV), which containsacoreCpGislandelement(IE)betweentheenhancerand core promoter to drive the expression of the three genes [30, 31]. By taking advantage of the lower translation efficiency oftheIRES-drivengenethanthegenedirectlydownstreamofthe promoter, wearrangedtheLCgeneasthefirstcistronandtheHC geneasthesecondcistroninthetricistronicvectortoexpressexcess

LC polypeptides. Expressing extra LC is beneficial for enhancing mAb expression level and reducing aggregate [11]. The selection marker gene in this tricistronic vector is dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR),whichhasbothselectionandgeneamplificationfunction and works best in DHFR deficient CHO DG44 cells. To improve the stringency of selection for high-producing cells, a mutated IRES with attenuated strength (IRESatt) was applied on DHFR to reduce its expression, allowing only clones with the plasmid vectorsamplifiedtohighcopiestosurvivetheselection[32]. 2 Materials 2.1 Plasmid 1. pIEDattvector. Production, Purification, and Characterization of Antibody-TNF Superfamily Ligand Fusion Proteins Martin Siegemund, Nadine Beha, and Dafne Mu¨ller Abstract Antibody-fusionproteinswithligands, e.g.,oftheTNFsuperfamily(TNFSF)canbeadequatelyproduced inmammalianexpressionsystems. Here, wedescribethetransientproductioninadherentandsuspension humanembryonickidneycellsatlaboratoryscale, followedbypurificationproceduresapplyingproteinA and immobilized metal affinity chromatography for proteins with Fc domain and 6 histidine-tag, respectively. In addition, characterization of the purified proteins by size exclusion chromatography is described. Keywords Antibody-fusionprotein, Fcfusion, IMAC, ProteinA, Sizeexclusionchromatography 1 Introduction Antibodyengineeringhasoriginatedalargevarietyof formatsthat can be furthermore fused with other proteins, e.g., ligands and cytokines, extending their range of potential applications [1, 2]. This implicates the generation of molecules of increased complexity, often glycosylated, that require the production in eukaryotic expression systems. Since optimization of formats and linkersareoftenneededtoobtainafusionproteinwiththedesired properties, fast production and purification procedures at laboratory scale become essential. Here, transient expression in human embryonic kidney (HEK) cells is considered a good option, since they can be efficiently transfected with plasmid DNA complexed, e.g., with cationic polymers and are known as high producer cells [3,4]. Fusion of proteins with an Fc domain is commonly used to improve the physicochemical and pharmaceutical properties, e.g., by inducing dimerization and serum half-life extension, and benefits from easy expression and purification [5, 6]. For Fc-fusion proteins, classicalpurificationbyproteinAaffinitychromatography is usually the first choice, being one of the most employed affinity

352 MartinSiegemundetal. purification systems because of its high selectivity and improved robustness [7]. Fusion proteins with small recombinant antibody fragments, e.g., single-chain variable fragment (scFv), commonly incorporate affinity tags for purification like polyhistidine-tag, Strep-tag, andFLAG-tagamongothers[8].Ingeneral, theclassical 6 histidine-tag can be placed conveniently at the N- or C-terminus of the fusion protein or even in between the fusion partners. An easy to establish purification procedure by immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) and the broad availability of appropriate detection antibodies make it a reliable toolforpreclinicalapplications, althoughthereisapotentialriskof influencing biophysical properties and immunogenicity [9] that rules it out for further clinical applications. Finally, size exclusion chromatography(SEC)isavaluabletooltocharacterizeantibodyligandfusionproteinsundernativeconditions, whereseparationby molecular size provides not only information about the hydrodynamic radius and the apparent molecular mass but also even more important, aboutthecompositionintermsofoligomerandaggregateformationthatcanhaveanimpactontheactivityofantibodyfusionproteins, especiallywithTNFSFmembers, e.g.,TRAILand 4-1BBL. In this case, trimer formation constitutes an intrinsic property of this family, and oligomerization is an important factor for activity display [10]. Here, the generation of the single-chain format(scTNFSF),i.e.,consecutivefusionofthreeectodomainsof the TNFSF member using peptide linkers, has shown to facilitate the design and generation of corresponding antibody-fusion proteins[11,12]. Here, wedescribetwoproductionandpurificationmethodsfor the generation of Fc-scTRAIL and scFv-sc4-1BBL fusion proteins at a lab scale: (1) transient production in adherent HEK293 cells followed by protein A affinity chromatography and (2) transient production in HEK293-6E suspension cells, followed by IMAC purification, respectively. Furthermore, a protocol for the analysis of antibody-fusion proteins by size exclusion chromatography is provided. 2 Materials 2.1 Transient 1. Chemoenzymatic Defucosylation of Therapeutic Antibodies for Enhanced Effector Functions Using Bacterial α-Fucosidases Chao Li, Tiezheng Li, and Lai-Xi Wang Abstract Corefucosylationplaysacriticalroleinmodulatingtheeffectorfunctionsoftherapeuticantibodiessuchas theantibody-dependentcellularcytotoxicity(ADCC)throughadverselyaffectingtheaffinityofantibodies forFcγreceptors.Thus, afacilemethodforFcdefucosylationofantibodiesisimportantbothforfunctional studies and for an enhanced therapeutic efficacy. In this chapter, we describe a detailed protocol for chemoenzymatic defucosylation of antibodies using Herceptin (trastuzumab) as a model system. The protocolincludes(a)FcdeglycosylationusingendoglycosidaseS2(Endo-S2);(b)enzymaticdefucosylation of the resulting Fucα1,6GlcNAc-Herceptin using two distinct bacterial α-fucosidases, AlfC and BfFuc; (c) transglycosylation of the GlcNAc-Herceptin using an Endo-S2 mutant (Endo-S2 D184M) as the enzymeandacomplexN-glycanoxazolineasthedonorsubstrate;and(d)SPRanalysisofthebindingof antibody glycoforms with the FcγIIIA receptor. The protocol of enzymatic defucosylation of Herceptin shouldbeequallyapplicablefortheFcglycanengineeringofothermAbs. Key words Therapeutic antibody, Chemoenzymatic synthesis, Glycoengineering, α-Fucosidase, Defucosylation, Transglycosylation, ADCC 1 Introduction Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) of the immunoglobulin G (IgG) class are an important class of therapeutic agents widely used for the treatment of cancer, autoimmune diseases, and infectious diseases [1, 2]. The IgG-type antibodies consist of two identical Fab domains responsible for antigen binding and the Fc domain that interacts with Fc receptors to mediate antibody effector functions. TheFcdomainofallIgGspossessesaconservedN-glycosylationsite towhichabiantennarycomplex-typeglycanistypicallyattached, but significant structural heterogeneity arises from terminal and core modifications, including variations in terminal galactosylation and sialylation, additionofbisectingN-acetylglucosamine(GlcNAc),and corefucosylation[3].Compellingdatahavedemonstratedthatcore

368 ChaoLietal. fucosylation, the attachment of an α1,6-linked fucose to the innermostGlcNAcmoietyoftheFcN-glycans, significantlydecreasesthe affinity of antibodies for the FcγIIIA receptor on effector cells, leading to dramatically reduced antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) [4–6]. However, antibodies produced from various host expression systems are usually core-fucosylated. Thus one way to enhance the ADCC-based therapeutic efficacy is to produce antibodies with low Fc fucose content. Recently, two glycoengineered mAbs with low fucose content were approved by the FDA that showedenhanced therapeuticefficacy in anticancer treatment. Oneis the mogamulizumab (POTELIGEO)producedin an engineered CHO cell line in which the α1,6-fucosyltransferase (FUT8) responsible for core fucosylation was knocked out [7]. The other is the obinutuzumab (Gazyva) produced from the CHOcelllinesoverexpressingtheβ1,4-GlcNActransferaseIII(GnT III), which overexpresses a bisecting GlcNAc moiety that prevents furthercorefucosylationoftheFcN-glycans[8]. As an alternative approach to Fc defucosylation through the engineeringofhostexpressionsystems, Wangandco-workershave recently developed a chemoenzymatic glycan remodeling method that allows an efficient in vitro Fc glycan engineering of existing intacttherapeuticantibodiestoproducehomogeneousglycoforms [9–11].Themethodconsistsoftwokeysteps:theFcdeglycosylation of an antibody with an endoglycosidase such as the endoglycosidaseS(Endo-S)fromStreptococcuspyogenesandthesubsequent enzymatic reglycosylation using a glycosynthase mutant such as Endo-S D233A to afford a homogeneous glycoform of the antibody [9–11]. More recently, novel glycosynthase mutants were generated from Endo-S2 that demonstrated much enhanced catalytic efficiency over the Endo-S enzyme. In combination with the use of an α-fucosidase, non-fucosylated glycoforms of antibodies could be generated, that showed much higher ADCC than the originalantibodies[12,13]. We have previously described the general protocols for the chemoenzymatic glycoengineering of intact antibodies to produce homogeneous antibody glycoforms [14, 15]. In this paper, we describeadetailedprotocolofthechemoenzymaticdefucosylation of Herceptin (i.e., trastuzumab, a mAb drug widely used for the treatmentofbreastcancer)asamodelsystemwiththefocusonthe comparisonofdefucosylationbytwobacterialα-fucosidases. Oneis the α-fucosidase AlfC from Lactobacillus casei that shows both hydrolysis and transglycosylation activity [16–18]. The other is the α-fucosidase BfFuc from Bacteroides fragilis that demonstrates verybroadsubstratespecificity[12,13].Theschematicprocedures are shown in Fig. 1. The protocol includes (1) Fc deglycosylation using the endoglycosidase S2 (Endo-S2); (2) enzymatic defucosylation of the resulting Fucα1,6GlcNAc-Herceptin by two distinct bacterial α-fucosidases, the AlfC and BfFuc; (3) reglycosylation of

Fc Glycoand Fc Protein-Engineering: Design of Antibody Variants with Improved ADCC and CDC Activity Christian Kellner, Stefanie Derer, Katja Klausz, Sophia Rosskopf, Tim Wirt, Thies Ro¨sner, Anna Otte, Elisa Cappuzzello, and Matthias Peipp Abstract Monoclonal antibodies are established treatment options in cancer therapy. However, not all patients benefit from antibody therapy. Basic research and findings from clinical trials revealed that certain Fc-mediatedeffectormechanismstriggeredbymonoclonalantibodiesareessentialforefficientantitumor activity. Today, next-generation monoclonalantibodiescanbedesigneddisplayingtailor-madeimproved effector functions. The introduction of Fc-engineering technologies offers the potential to fine-tune Fc-mediatedeffectorfunctionssuchasantibody-dependentcell-mediatedcytotoxicity(ADCC),phagocytosis, or complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC). Fc-engineered antibodies hopefully will overcome somelimitationsofcurrentformsofantibodytherapy. Keywords Antibodyengineering, ADCC, CDC 1 Introduction Monoclonal antibodies are widely applied in cancer therapy in various clinical settings [1]. Despite their documented clinical activity, not all patients benefit from established antibody-based immunotherapies. Preclinical and clinical data suggest important rolesforimmune-mediatedeffector functionsinantibodytherapy. Therefore, antibody engineering approaches with the goal in improvingtheinteractionoftheantibodyFcdomainwithcomponents of the patients’ immune system may overcome some limitationsofconventionalantibodytherapy. | | | To | date, human | IgG1 is | the most commonly | used antibody | | | — | — | — | ———– | ——- | —————– | ————- | — | isotype in cancer therapy. Therefore, various antibody engineering approacheshavebeendevelopedtomodulatetheeffectorfunctions of this isotype [2]. Antibodies with tailor-made effector functions can be realized by the so-called Fc glyco-engineering, Fc proteinengineering, or a combination of both. Sidhu, and Donghui Wu Abstract The therapeutic efficacy of an antibody drug depends on the variable domains and on the constant crystallizablefragment(Fc).IgGvariabledomainshavebeenthetargetsofextensivemolecularengineering in search of more specific binders with higher affinities for their targets. Similarly, Fc engineering approacheshaveledtomodulatingboththeimmuneeffectorresponsesandserumhalf-livesoftherapeutic antibodies. A high-affinity interaction between the IgG Fc and neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) at aslightly acidicpHcanprotectIgGmoleculesfromundergoinglysosomalorserumproteinase-induceddegradation. Herewedescribeanoptimizedprotocolforthedevelopmentofatailored, synthetichumanFcrepertoireto selectFcmutantswhichshowhighlypH-restrictedFcRnbindingwithhighaffinity. Keywords Antibody, Fc,FcRn, Serumhalf-life, Affinity, Phagedisplay, Tailored, Syntheticlibrary 1 Introduction IgG antibody drugs are the most successful classes of biological molecules currently in clinical use [1]. Their success can be attributed, inpart, tothefactthattheycanbedevelopedusingstandard molecular engineering techniques [2–6], are generally welltolerated, show a better safety profile, and have higher approval rates than small molecules [7]. The crystallizable fragment (Fc) of IgGsubclassesisinvolvedin(1)immuneeffectoractivationwhich decreasesintheorderofIgG3>IgG1>IgG4>IgG2[8,9]and (2)serumlongevitywhichvaries from~23days(IgG1,IgG2,and IgG4) down to 7–21 days (IgG3; depending on allotypes which contain either arginine or histidine at position 435) [9–11]. One approach to enhance the pharmacological properties of IgG drugs is to optimize binding of the Fc with neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) Fcγ for desired serum half-life and receptors for desired immune functions [12, 13]. By molecular evolution, some IgG therapies have enhanced efficacy regarding immune functions and serum

400 AbhishekSaxenaetal. half-life, for example, in the treatment of cancer/microbial infections or inflammatory conditions, and as vehicles to deliver cytotoxicor radioactivepayloads[13–23]. The maintenance of serum IgG levels is an outcome of a pH-dependentinteractionbetweenFcandFcRnwhichisexpressed inendothelial, epithelial, andhematopoieticcells[13,24].FcRnis atransmembraneheterodimericproteinconsistingofanextracellular heavy chain (with three domains; α1, α2 and α3), a transmembrane region, and a short cytoplasmic domain [25, 26]. A single unit of soluble beta-2-microglobulin (β2M) associates with the FcRn heavy chain non-covalently. Residues within the cytoplasmic domain of rat FcRn are involved in FcRn endocytosis from the plasmamembraneandbasolateraltransport[25,27].Maintenance of Ig-FcRn interactions at pH 6.0 favors endosomal trafficking of the complex away from the lysosomal degradation pathway, recycling it instead to the plasma membrane where IgG is re-released into the blood at pH 7.4. This mechanism provides an increased IgG half-life in blood, which is necessary for extended exposure of the antibody to its target and enhanced potential for therapeuticefficacy. Intermolecular interactions between Fc and FcRn that influence IgG homeostasis have been mapped in considerable detail by mutational and structural studies [23, 28–36, 37–39]. Histidine residuespresentinthehumanFc(atpositions310,433,and436) are responsible for pH-restricted interactions [23, 29, 30, 31, 39]. Studies have also shown that residues M252, I253, S254, T256,N434,H435,M428,andY436inhumanFcareimportant contributors to Fc-FcRn binding [23, 29, 30, 36]. Here, we describe a method to develop a diverse Fc repertoire based on tailored mutations in three regions important for binding to FcRn. The diversities were introduced into a previously described human IgG1-Fc mutant (M252Y/S254T/T256E, short for hu- Fc-YTE hereafter) that was isolated from a phage-displayed syntheticlibrary[29].Thehu-Fc-YTEbindshumanandmonkeyFcRn withapproximatelytenfoldhigheraffinityincomparisontoFcwild type (Fc-WT) at pH 6.0 [17, 29]. Furthermore, YTE mutations when introduced into a humanized anti-respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)monoclonalantibody, increasedtheIgGhalf-lifebyfourfold incynomolgusmonkey[17]. TofurtheridentifyimprovedFcmutants, weadoptedanaffinitymaturationstrategybasedonFc-YTEtemplatebyretainingthe Y252andT256mutations andintroducingnovelresidues atpositions 253, 254, 309, 311, 433, 434, and 436 in order to further enhancetheFcaffinityforFcRn.Wepresentdetailedprotocolsfor theconstructionofaphage-displayedhumanFcmutantlibraryand forinvitroselectionofhigh-affinityFcbinderstoFcRnspecifically at pH 6.0. We used Kunkel’s method [40] to incorporate tailored diversities in designated regions of Fc. Uracil-containing, single-
