Characterization, Optimization, and Innovative Formats

Chapter 22

Measuring Antibody-Antigen Binding Kinetics Using Surface Plasmon Resonance Stephen Hearty, Paul Leonard, Hui Ma, and Richard O’Kennedy Abstract Surfaceplasmonresonance(SPR)isnowwidelyembracedasatechnologyformonitoringadiverserangeof protein-protein interactions and is considered almost de rigueur for characterizing antibody-antigen interactions. The technique obviates the need to label either of the interacting species, and the binding eventisvisualizedinrealtime. Thus, itisideallysuitedforscreeningcrude, unpurifiedantibodysamples that dominate early candidate panels following antibody selection campaigns. SPR returns not only concentrationandaffinitydatabutwhenusedcorrectlycanresolvethediscretecomponentkineticparameters (association and dissociation rate constants) of the affinity interaction. Herein, we outline some SPR-basedgenericantibodyscreeningconfigurationsandmethodologiesinthecontextofexpeditingdatarich ranking of candidate antibody panels and ensuring that antibodies with the optimal kinetic binding characteristicsarereliablyidentified. Keywords Surfaceplasmonresonance(SPR),Antibody, Affinity, Antigen, Associationrate, Dissociationrate, Screening 1 Introduction Thekeyattributesofantibodiesarespecificityandaffinity, asthese will largely dictate the overall functional performance metrics whether in a therapeutic or diagnostic setting. Breaking this combinationdownintoitsmostbasicinterpretation, itmayfeasiblybe argued that specificity is simply a manifestation of greater affinity for an antigenic singularity over the plurality of the broader antigeniclandscape[1]. 1.1 AntibodyAffinity The natural immune repertoire is a dynamic system with affinity maturation potentiated through environmental antigen exposure or stimulated by immunization. Estimated repertoire sizes are in theorderof108,althoughthisisdifficulttoaccuratelydefinedueto the plasticity of the repertoire. In theory, the immune system has the capacity to continually evolve and mature antibodies to

422 StephenHeartyetal. exquisitely high affinity, but this does not actually manifest in vivo where antibodies isolated by hybridoma or B cell immortalization techniques do not generally return antibodies below single-digit nanomolar affinity. This has previously been attributed to the theorizedexistenceofanaffinityceiling[2],thecentraltenetofwhich maintains that although the immune system has the capacity to generate ultrahigh affinity, there is no negative selection pressure to remove weaker binding antibodies below the proposed affinity ceiling(~100pM)invivo. ThisisbasedontheassertionthattheB cell receptor (BCR) on-rate (k ) for cognate monomeric antigen on cannot be faster than the maximum rate of diffusion, and thus in vivo selection based on off-rate (k ) can only be countenanced off withinthelimitoftheantigeninternalizationrate. Thisisprobably an oversimplification as it does not consider avidity or conformationaltwo-statebindingeventsthatareinfactkeyfacetsofparticulate and immobilized antigen binding [3]. Likewise, somatic hypermutationisastochasticprocessthatisitselfentirelyindependent of the thermodynamic and kinetic constraints of any affinity ceiling. Thus, on these terms it would appear that the true affinity potentialofthenaturalimmunerepertoirecannotbefullyrealized andsampledinvitro. However, advancesincombinatorialantibody library generation and display technologies have largely overcome this significant hurdle. The diversity of combinatorial antibody libraries can greatly exceed that of the natural immune repertoire, and the heavy-light chain pairings are truly randomized [4]. In vitro, we are not subject to the same kinetic binding constraints that prevail in BCR evolution in vivo, and thus it is theoretically possible to isolate very high-affinity binders from immune combinatorial libraries. It would appear that the traditional antibody ceiling is being raised, with affinities in the femtomolar range being reported for certain anti-hapten antibodies [5]. Affinity data alone often carries insufficient discriminatory weight as the keydifferentiatorinmanycomplexinvivoindicationswilllikelybe dominated by either or both the discrete component k and k on off parameterssuchaswasdemonstratedinthecaseofapanelofanti- SIVenvelope antibodies with similar K values but variable neu- D tralizationpotencyproportionaltoincreaseink andk [6]. on off 1.2 SurfacePlasmon For any antibody generation campaign, it is of paramount impor- Resonance(SPR) tance to differentiatethe most promising candidates (i.e., highestaffinity binders) as early in the campaign as possible. Doing this solely on the basis of measurements from direct ELISA signal is subject to variation arising from the disparity in expression levels and functional stability. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR), a standard biophysical characterization tool for measuring ligand binding, has emerged as a key technology for examining antibody-antigen interactions, due ostensibly to thefact that bindingevents can be monitored in “real time” and without the requirement for

MeasuringAntibody-AntigenBinding 423 Shifted Resonance angle Resonance angle Prism Prism Sensor chip Gold film Antibody Antigen Antibody Flow cell Flow cell Fig. 1 SPR detection system. This example shows how antibodies are immobilized onto the sensor chip surfaceoftheflowcell. Antigensarethenpassedovertheantibodysurface, whichcausesamasschangeand thenleadstoashiftofresonanceanglethatcorrespondstothebindingantigenconcentration ligand or analyte labeling. These key attributes facilitate accurate kinetic measurements and rapid analysis and reduce the additional costsandpossibleheterogeneitiesorothercomplicationsassociated withlabelingofinteractants[7]. Thepurposeofthischapteristoprovideanaccountoftreatise in the application of SPR technology to screening and analysis of recombinant antibodies, and we seek not to overly concern ourselves with the complex physico-optical theory underpinning this key enabling technology. Things have progressed greatly from 30yearsagowhenSPRtechnologywasstillinitsinfancy, underexploited, andthepreserveofopticalandphysicaltheorists. Here, we will concern ourselves with the practical application (and issues affectingperformanceanddesigncriteria)rather thantheunderlying physico-optical theory. Suffice to say that SPR is a powerful technologythatmeasuresrefractiveindex(RI)changesatorproximal(100nm)toametal(generallygold)surface, potentiatedby ligand binding and concomitant localized mass changes. It is a superlative technology for measuring protein-protein interactions and is widely embraced by both academic and biopharmaceutical antibodyresearchpractitioners. Infact, supportingSPRdataisnow consideredalmostderigueurinanyantibodygenerationcampaign. Afterantibody-antigenbindingonthesensorsurface, anincreaseof massatthesensorsurfacewillbeobserved, followedbyalterations in the refractive index and finally the shift of the resonance angle. Theshiftoftheresonanceanglewillberecordedandconvertedto resonance units (RU) in real time (Fig. 1) [8]. One thousand RU represent an approximate 0.1 shift of resonance angle, which corresponds to a change in surfaceprotein concentration of about 1ng/mm2[9].

The buffer should be allowed to equilibrate to room temperature and prepared freshly before each samplerun. 3 Methods 3.1 Instrument Cleaning and routine maintenance are a key contributor to good- Cleaning quality SPR data whatever instrument is used. It is important to sanitizetheinstrumentfluidicsfrequently, particularlyiftheinstrument is continuously exposed to crude biological matrices. Likewise, it is recommended to “desorb” the fluidics before and after each screening campaign to prevent fouling with proteinacious materialsusingaprotocolsuchasthefollowing: 1. Settheinstrumenttemperatureto25 C. 2. Dock a maintenance chip in the instrument. This is a bare sensorchipwithoutanattachedCMdextranlayer. 3. “Prime” the instrument five times with “desorb solution 1” (0.5%sodiumdodecylsulfate[SDS]). 4. Primeoncewithwater. 5. Prime five times with “desorb solution 2” (50 mM glycine, pH9.5). 6. Finally, primefivetimeswithwater. 3.2 ChipSelection There are a variety of chips available. By far the most frequently usedandmostmalleableistheCM5chip.Thiscomprisesacarboxymethylateddextran(CMdextran)-coatedsurface, whichfacilitates covalent attachmentat the carboxylgroup and isparticularly amenabletocovalentimmobilizationofproteins, includingantibodies, via intrinsic lysine amino groups. More specialized surfaces are available, e.g., hydrophobic (HPA chip) and lipophilic (L1 chip) surfacesfor membraneintegration, and maybeusefulfor mimickingmembranedisplayandscreeningforantibodybindingtomembrane contextually dependent epitopes. A dedicated streptavidin-coated “SA chip” and nitrilotriacetic acid-coated “NTA chip” are also available for capture of biotinylated or His-tagged ligands, respectively.

430 StephenHeartyetal. 3.3 Immobilization The process of ligand immobilization can be performed by (a) direct covalent attachment or (b) ligand capture. The former canproduceverystable, regenerabletestsurfacesassumingthatthe ligand itself tolerates the chemical immobilization process and regeneration conditions. Conversely, the latter strategy is more applicable to generic platform screening analysis since the ligand itself can be varied between analysis cycles and is accordingly the formatofchoiceforscreeninglargepanelantibodies, particularlyin theearly-phasescreenwhenthecandidateantibodiesarelikelytobe crude and unpurified. It is important to have a generic capture platform to seamlessly accommodate multiple independent antibody campaigns. In the absence of a high-throughput (HT) purification step [41], it is clearly not possible to selectively covalentlyconjugateeachcandidateantibodyontoadedicatedchip surface, norisitcost-ortime-effective! Byusinganaffinitycapture approach, theligandpreparationsneednotbesubjecttoprescreening purification because the ligand will be reliably captured and faithfully displayed through an affinity tag or domain compatible withthecaptureligand. “Off-the-shelf”genericcapturesurfacesincludetheSAchipfor capture of biotinylated ligand. The high affinity of the biotin-SA interactionrenderscapturebythismethodtobeeffectivelynonreversibleandnon-regenerable(seeNote1).Moreover, biotinylation of early campaign antibody candidates whether by site-specific invivo[42]orinvitrochemicalconjugationisnotroutinelyundertaken. Capture of His-tagged antibodies is a more commonly employed alternative strategy and is readily accommodated on the NTA sensor chip surface. However, we prefer our experience suggestsvariableperformance, nonstandardbuffer, andsurfacepreparation/regeneration requirements (see Note 2). Additionally, His-tagged antibodies may vary in the steric accessibility of their respective His-tag, and the presence of competing histidine-rich proteinswithinantibodysamplespresentincrudelysatesorculture supernatant may lead to non-specific binding events that are difficult to countenance by standard referencing protocols. It is also importanttonotethatifaHis-tagligandcaptureapproachisused, itwillprecludethepossibilityofusingaHis-taggedantigenpreparationastheanalytespecies. Undoubtedly, the most broadly applicable strategy involves preparing a dedicated capture surface by immobilizing a suitable high-affinity capture ligand compatible with an affinity tag or sequence expressed in each of the antibody constructs within a particular screening campaign or series of campaigns. If the antibody constructs are full IgG molecules, then protein A or anti-Fc antibody [43] are obvious and proven capture ligand options. In the case of recombinant antibodies, particularly minimalist fragments such as single-chain fragment variable (scFv) constructs, it isoftenthestandardpracticetoincludeadefinedtagsequencefor

Accordingly, thepHof the coupling buffer must be appropriate to induce an overall net positivechargeontheligand. Intuitively, thelower thepHrelative to the pI of the ligand, the greater the positive charge will be. However, as the ligand will be exposed to coupling buffer for an extended period during immobilization (typically 15–30 min), one cannot just arbitrarily select a very acidic pH due to the likelihood of denaturation. Furthermore, EDC-NHSmediated carbodiimide conjugation has a relatively narrow pH range in which it performs optimally. Nonetheless, even small differences in pH can haveadramaticimpactoncouplingefficiency, andthusitisnecessary to determine this value empirically using a preconcentration scouting experiment. The preconcentration is driven by electrostatic interactions, and this is most dramatic in low ionic strength buffers. This is particularly important when dealing with crude or complexsamplemediasuchaslysates, cellextracts, orculturemedia, suchasismostfrequentintheearly-phasescreeningofrecombinant antibodypanels. IntheBiacore3000instrument, samplesarepassed acrosstheflowcellsinseriessothatimmobilizationofligandonflow

434 StephenHeartyetal. cells 2 and 4 facilitates dedication of flow cells 1 and 3 as control surfaces and enables both 2-1 and 4-3 referencing configurations. For screening purposes, it is also possible to immobilize ligand on flowcells2,3,and4andreferencethesechannelsagainstthesingle control surface. The control surface options include (a) a blank, untreated CM dextran surface, (b) an activated and “capped” surface(i.e.,asurfacethathasbeenactivatedandthencappedwithout post-activationexposuretoligand),and(c)adummyligandsurface (i.e., a surface to which a surrogate non-analyte-binding ligand is immobilized).Inthelattercase, itisimportantthatthe“dummy” ligandissuitablyrepresentativeoftheactiveligandsurfaceinterms ofsize, charge, etc. Forcapture-basedassays, anadditionalcontrol surfaceoptionarises. Thiscomprisesareferencesurfaceontowhich captureligandisalsoimmobilizedatasimilarleveltotheactivetest surface. However, testligandisonlydirectedtothetestsurfacewith analyte sample then passed across both the ligand-occupied test surface and the ligand-unoccupied reference surface. On the Biacore 3000 instrument, this can be achieved using the “FLOW- PATH” command. Many users opt to routinely use the simple “blank” surface option. Whichever option is favored, it is prudent toconductthefollowingseriesofchecks: 1. Test for binding of ligand sample to control surface (if not usingunoccupiedcapturesurfaceascontrol). 2. Test for binding of sample matrix (e.g., ligand-deficient spent supernatant or cell lysate) to the control surface, ligand-occupied capture surface, and the ligand-unoccupied capture surface. 3. Testforbindingofanalytetocontrolsurface. 4. Test for binding of analyte to the ligand-unoccupied capture surface. If no gross artifactual or aberrant binding responses (see Note 14) are noted, then it is possible to proceed with confidence to kineticbindinganalysis. 3.5 SampleBuffer It is important that the sample buffer should match the running Considerations: bufferascloselyaspossiblesoastopreventlargebulkRIchangesat the start and end of sample injections and ensure that dissociation and association proceed under identical conditions. The default buffer of choice is HBS containing 3 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, ® and surfactant (e.g., 0.005–0.05% (v/v) Tween 20) to minimize non-specific electrostatic and hydrophobic binding to the chip surface. Thesealsohelpmaintaintheanalyteinanoptimallysoluble state and minimize aggregation propensity and sample depletion through adsorption to reagent vials and tubing. In certain userdefinedcases, itmaybepreferabletousePBSinsteadofHBSasthe sample buffer, and in such cases the running buffershould also be changed to PBS. Some analytes may exhibit characteristics that

MeasuringAntibody-AntigenBinding 435 dictate special buffer considerations. For example, metal ion-dependent analytes (e.g., Ca++ or Mg++) may require supplementationwithcompatiblemetalsaltsandomissionofEDTAfrom boththesampleandrunningbuffers. In the case of affinity capture of test ligands (e.g., antibody library screening), where the antibodies are not purified prior to analysisandareprovidedascrudelysateorculturesupernatantand non-specific binding is suspected, the ligand should be diluted in running buffer supplemented with 12 mg/mL BSA and 12 mg/ mLCMdextransodiumsalt. 3.6 Regeneration Themajoradvantageofusinganaffinitycapturestrategytocapture candidate antibodies is that the capture is reversible and thus it is possible to reuse the surface repeatedly for analysis of multiple candidate antibodies. Both the reproducibility of the binding data and the lifetime of a particular chip surface will be dictated by the choiceofregenerationconditionsemployed. Thecorollarytothisis that once conditions are optimized for a particular capture ligand, they do not have to be re-optimized for subsequent antibody screening campaigns using the same affinity capture system. By simply serially injecting a fixed concentration of capture target (in this case candidate antibody with a HA tag sequence) interdigitated with a pulse of test regeneration solution and monitoring the target capture level between regeneration pulses and the baseline level after each regeneration pulse, the test regeneration solution yielding the most stable and reproducible target capture level andbaselineresponseisdetermined(Fig.5). We generally prefer to use no more than a 30s pulse of regeneration solution to minimize exposure time at the ligand surface, and for antibody-mediated affinity capture, we find that freshly prepared 5–50 mM NaOH (see Note 15) is widely effective and ensures acceptable chip lifetime. Many users opt to use acidic regeneration conditions such as glycine-HCl; however, this can often require an extended post-regeneration baseline stabilization periodbetweensampleanalyses. 3.7 Measuring Mass transfer limitation (MTL) [44] is one of the most frequent BindingKinetics causesofcomplications inperformingany kineticexperimentona surface-bound ligand. However, it is also one of the easiest pro-3.7.1 MassTransfer blems to identify and address through experimental design. The mass a transfercomponentisdefinedbytheflowrate, flowcelldimensions (height, h;width, w;andlength, l),andthediffusioncoefficientof the analyte (D). Since h, w, and l are fixed parameters and D is

The baseline (pink)andbindingresponse(blue)levelswererecordedduringtheperformanceofsixbindingcyclesforeach regenerationbuffer. Inordertochooseagoodregenerationbuffer, thebaselineandbindingresponsesshould beconsistentforeachcycle. Adjacent spots (1 + 2 + 3 and 4 + 5) are activated at the same time, but the delay between activation and immobilization onthe innerspots (2+ 4)as opposedto the outer spots (1 + 5) means that the inner spots are exposed to hydrolysis for a longer period and thus the percentage of active esters is reduced. This manifests in a lower coupling efficiency and consequently, lowerlevelsofimmobilizedcaptureligand. Thiseffectwill be most pronounced when standard running buffer (pH 7.4) is usedintheimmobilizationprocedure. Conversely, usinglowerpH runningbuffer(10mMacetate,150mMNaCl,0.05%(v/v)P20, pH 4.5) during the immobilization run will reduce the degree of hydrolysis (see Note 24) with a concomitant greater retention of couplingefficiency. For direct covalent immobilization, it is difficult to precisely fixthetargetligandimmobilizationlevelsinceitisnonreversible and cannot be achieved by iterative titration. Moreover, the % functionality of the immobilized ligand is even more difficult to predict. A generic regenerable capture approach facilitates iterative titration of the test antibody to determine the appropriate antibody dilution to use, and the oriented capture also serves to maximize functionality and reduces possibleligandheterogeneityonthesurface.

However, na¨ıvebindingdomainsoftensufferfromlow targetaffinity. Inaddition, constructionoflargena¨ıvelibrariesresultsinnon-nativepairingofheavyand lightv-domainswhichcanpresentachallengetomolecularstability. Herewedescribeeffectivemethodsfor theparallelevolutionofantibodyaffinityandthermalstabilitywhichcouplemutantantibodylibraryphage displaywithcarefullydesignedselectionstrategies. Key words Affinity optimization, Thermal stability, scFv, Mutagenesis, Phage display, Selection strategy 1 Introduction The molecular engineering of antibodies and antibody fragments has progressed significantly in recent years. Blinatumomab is a bi-specific, single-chain antibody comprising an anti-CD19 scFv | | | linked in tandem | | with | an anti-CD3 | scFv for | T-cell | engagement | | — | — | —————- | — | —- | ———– | ——– | —— | ———- | that is proving very efficacious in acute lymphoblastic leukemia patientpopulations[1,2].Itsmolecular formatislowincomplexity, representing a single polypeptide chain that greatly simplifies scale-upexpressionand purification. Thisiscoupledwithanintravenousrouteofadministrationatarelativelylowdose, thusnegating the requirement for high concentration formulation. The potentialforsubcutaneousdosingathighconcentrationinchronic inflammatory indications would be highly desirable; however, development of scFv-based therapeutics for these indications has been hampered by issues associated with low stability and high aggregation propensity. Stability optimization ofv-domain pairing

458 EdwardFranklinetal. has been approached through modulation of domain orientation andlinkers[3,4],introductionofinterchaindisulfidebonds[5,6], and rational engineering of framework/VH–VL interface residues basedoncomputationalmodelling[7,8].However, manyofthese methods involve introduction of nonnatural amino acid sequence or mutation in what are generally highly conserved framework regions. Thismayleadtosequenceliabilitiesassociatedwithdownstream developability challenges or introduction of non-germline T-cellepitopeswhichcanincreasetheriskforADAresponses. Large na¨ıve scFv fragment libraries coupled with display technologiesremainaworkhorseforantigen-bindingdomaindiscovery efforts across the industry. However, these na¨ıve binding domains often suffer from low affinity coupled with low thermal stability, some of which results from suboptimal v-domain pairing introduced during library construction. Herein, we describe tailored selection strategies which allow the parallel optimization of both antibodyaffinityandthermalstabilitywhilerestrictingallmutagenesis to the naturally diverse complementarity-determining regions (CDRs). TheschematicpresentedinFig.1summarizesthekeystepsfor the parallel evolution of antibody affinity (in this case in scFv format) and the thermal stability optimization discussed in Subheading 3. This encompasses CDR-based mutagenesis (Subheading3.1),thecloningofscFv-phagemidlibraries(Subheading3.2), phagelibraryrescue(Subheading3.3),phageselectionsforaffinity improvement(Subheading3.4),thermalshockselection(Subheading 3.5), and scFv expression (Subheading 3.6). Screening processes include homogenous time-resolved fluorescence competition assay (HTRF) for the identification of affinity-improved clones (Subheading 3.7) and, finally, a “cook and bind” enzyme-linkedimmunosorbentassay(ELISA)fortheidentification ofcloneswithimprovedthermalstability(Subheading3.8). 2 Materials AllfromSigma-Aldrichunlessotherwisestated. 2.1 PhageLibrary LiquidMedia: Generation 1. It is important to consider the biophysical properties of the antigen used before designing your selection strategy. For example, theantigen may have a particularly high pI. In order to avoid enrichment of opposite charge in CDR loops, an opposite charge “deselection” pressure is included. This eases concerns that selection outputs would be dominated by an excess of charge-based interactions, (e.g., salt bridges) leading toanunusuallyhighpIforthefinalantibody, whichmaycause broader specificity issues. For this reason, selections in this example were performed in the presence of a large excess of positivelychargedhistonesintheblockingbuffer. 10. Numerous methods exist for the efficient recombination and screening of libraries in order to identify antibodies with optimized characteristics, such as higher affinity, derived from relatedclonesobtainedfromphage, yeast, orhybridomatechnologies or mutagenesis techniques [10, 21, 22]. It is important, however, to consider other biophysical properties that impact the ability to develop an antibody as a therapeutic suchasthermalstability[4],nonspecificbindingandclearance [23], and propensity to aggregate in solution [24], as well as solubility, FcRnbinding, anddissociation. Antibodymutations arising from in vitro somatic hypermutation, as with in vivo B-cell maturation, fall within CDRs, in particular heavy chain CDR1 and CDR2 at the antigen-contacting residues highlightedinFig.1.Thepositionandidentityofthesemutations can negatively impact properties such as aggregation while simultaneously improving affinity. Up to a third of all somatic hypermutationeventsfalloutsideCDRregionsandcanhavea profound impact of stability and manufacturability. Care should be taken to recombine smaller libraries of mutations while simultaneously monitoring affinity, activity, and other pertinentbiophysicalattributes. Keywords Nanobodies, Solidphasepeptidesynthesis, Molecularimagingandtherapy, Radiopharmaceuticals, SortaseA 1 Introduction Thesuccessofmolecularimagingisacceleratedbytheuseofhighly specific targeting molecular probes such as antibodies or antibody fragments that detect and associate in vivo to specific markers of disease[1–3].Thesemarkersoftenhaveprognosticvalueandallow the identification of patients that would benefit from targeted treatments. Single-domain antibody fragments (also referred to as VHH or Nanobodies (Nbs)) that are isolated from immunized camelids have proven their efficacy in this respect [4]. Such Nbs havealreadybeenidentifiedagainstseveralspecificdiseasemarkers in the fields of oncology [5], diabetes [6], inflammation [7], atherosclerosis [8], etc. Their favorable characteristics such as high stability, small size (e.g., approximately 15 kDa), fast targeting, and rapid blood clearance allow high-contrast images to be obtained as early as 1 h after Nb administration.

The straightforward technology to identify target-specific Nbs is a very attractive tool for the generic development of new molecular probes[9]. | | In order | to | translate | the Nbs | to | the clinic, | it is | preferred to | | — | ——– | — | ——— | ——- | — | ———– | —– | ———— | obtain a homogenous, well-defined, and well-characterized pharmaceuticalproduct. Toproducesuchhomogenousproducts, asitespecificcouplingofthemolecular reagent, e.g.,biotin, fluorescent dye, bifunctional chelator, etc., to the Nb must be performed. Several approaches can be followed [10]; here we propose a site-specific conjugation of a molecular reagent by using the Sortase A enzyme, a transpeptidase of Staphylococcus aureus [11]. This enzyme will recognize a recognition site, e.g., LPETG, that is introduced at the C-terminal of the Nb. By cleavage of the bond betweenthethreonineandglycineresidue, atrihedralintermediate is formed. An oligopeptide, consisting of three glycine residues followed by a tyrosine and lysine residue, will act in a next step as a nucleophile and will attack the formed intermediate. RearrangementofthebondsresultsinfreeSortaseAenzymeandcoupledNb insolution, nexttounreactedNbandprobe.Viaatwo-steppurification process, immobilized metal ion affinity chromatography (IMAC) followed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), the coupledNbcanbepurified[12]. This book chapter provides the protocols for in-frame cloning of a nanobody of interest in an expression vector encoding the sortag (Fig. 1), and the expression and purification of the Nb equipped with this sortag. We also describe the synthesis of a GGGYK pentapeptide where the ε-amino group of lysine is used forconjugationofabifunctionalchelator, toactasaprobetoligate on the sortag (Figs. 2 and 3). Other amino acids can be introduced betweenthethreeglycinesandthetyrosineifnecessary. Thelysine is always located at the C-terminus, while the N-terminus should contain three glycines. The probe is synthesized via Fmoc-based solid phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) using rink amide resin. The synthesisisperformedbyfirstanchoringthelysine(Allocprotected onthesidechain)totheresin, followedbythesuccessivecouplings ofthetyrosineandthethreeglycineresidues, respectively. Thelast glycine residue is N-protected with a Boc group to avoid an extra deprotection step. Once the sequence is completed, the Alloc protecting group on the lysine is selectively deprotected, releasing a free amine onto which the chelator can be coupled. Finally, the peptide is fully deprotected and cleaved from the resin. The crude peptide is then purified giving rise to the final probe with high purity. Inthis ofNbs protocol the substrate is a Nb with a C-terminal sortag (see Subheading3.3)andtheprobeapentapeptidecontainingthreeglycine 3.5.1 Site-Specific residuesfollowedbyatyrosineandlysine(GGGYK).Thecommer- CouplingofaChelator cially available chelators are coupled via the functionalized NCS toNbsUsingSortaseA group to the amine of lysine of the pentapeptide (Fig. 5). The thiolate group of a cysteine residue, located in the active site of the Sortase A enzyme, will attack the carbonyl group between the threonine and glycine residue in the signal sequence forming a tetrahedral intermediate (Fig. 3). Histidine, also located in the active site, is then deprotonated by the amide group between the threonine and glycine, which leads to the formation of a thioacyl intermediate. On his turn, the histidine residue removes a proton fromthetriglycineamidegroup, whichallowstheprobe(GGGYK) to attack the thioacyl intermediate. This leads to a tetrahedral intermediate, which is rearranged to facilitate the release of the cysteine residue and the newly formed product (Nb-LPET- GGGYK-chelator). 1.
